Shekel The shekel was the basic Hebrew unit of weight, used above all for weighing silver and gold. What it was. The word comes from a Hebrew verb meaning “to weigh”. For most of the Old Testament there were no coins: silver was weighed out on scales, and the shekel was the standard weight. Abraham “weighed out” four hundred shekels for a burial field. The “shekel of the sanctuary” was the official standard kept by the priests, and it was divided into twenty gerahs. Coins called shekels came much later, after the exile; in Jesus’ day the silver shekel of Tyre was the coin the temple required. In today’s terms. A shekel weighed about 0.4 oz (11.5 g), roughly the weight of two US quarters. As money its value changed over the centuries. By New Testament times a silver shekel was worth about four denarii, that is, about four days’ wages for a labourer. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing that money was weighed helps you read Jeremiah buying a field and “weighing out” seventeen shekels as a pledge of hope. It also shows how cheaply Jesus was valued. The law set thirty shekels as the compensation for a slave gored by an ox, and Zechariah was paid the same insulting wage. Judas sold the Lord of glory for thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave. Genesis 23:16 Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants. Before coins, silver changed hands by weight, measured against the standard weights merchants used. Exodus 21:32 If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver Thirty shekels was the legal value placed on a slave’s life. Matthew 26:15 And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. Jesus was betrayed for the price of a slave, fulfilling Zechariah 11:12 to 13. The thirty pieces of silver show how little the world thought of Christ, who freely took the form of a servant for us.

Talent The talent was the largest unit of weight in the Bible, and a huge sum of money when it was silver or gold. What it was. A talent was a weight equal to sixty minas or about three thousand shekels. It was the load a man could carry, and it was used for large amounts of metal: the gold of Solomon’s yearly income, the tribute kings demanded, the bronze and silver of the tabernacle. In the New Testament it appears in two of Jesus’ parables as a vast sum of money. In today’s terms. A talent weighed about 75 lb (34 kg); estimates vary between about 58 and 80 lb (26 to 36 kg). A talent of silver was worth about six thousand denarii. Since a denarius was a day’s wage, one talent was something like twenty years’ pay for a labourer. Ten thousand talents would be beyond the earnings of many lifetimes, rather like owing billions today. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This turns the parable of the unforgiving servant into a shock. He was forgiven a debt he could never have repaid, ten thousand talents, yet he choked a fellow servant over a hundred denarii, about four months’ wages. Our debt of sin before God is like the first, and it is cancelled in Christ; how then can we refuse to forgive the smaller debts of others? In the parable of the talents, even one talent was a great trust. Our English word “talent”, meaning a gift or ability, comes from this parable. Matthew 18:24 When he began to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. Jesus chose an impossibly large figure to picture the debt of our sin. Matthew 25:15 To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Even one talent was a fortune, entrusted to be used for the master until he returned. 1 Kings 10:14 Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, Talents were used for vast quantities, here about 23 tonnes (25 US tons) of gold.

Mina The mina was a weight and sum of money between the shekel and the talent, worth about fifty shekels. What it was. The mina (sometimes spelled “maneh”) was a Babylonian and Hebrew weight. Usually fifty shekels made a mina and sixty minas a talent, though Ezekiel describes a mina of sixty shekels, and standards varied. The returning exiles gave five thousand minas of silver for rebuilding the temple. “MENE” in the writing on Belshazzar’s wall is the same word. In New Testament Greek a mina was a hundred drachmas. In today’s terms. A mina weighed about 1¼ lb (570 g). As money in Jesus’ time it was worth about a hundred denarii, that is, about a hundred days’ wages for a labourer, or roughly three or four months’ pay. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In the parable of the minas each servant receives the same modest but real sum, about three months’ wages, and is told to trade with it until his master returns. Unlike the talents, the gift is equal; what differs is faithfulness. Jesus told it because people thought the kingdom would appear at once. The King has gone to receive his kingdom and will return, and meanwhile his servants are to use what he has given them, the gospel itself, for his gain. Luke 19:13 Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ Each servant received one mina, about a hundred days’ wages, to trade with. Luke 19:16 The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ The faithful servant gives the credit to the master’s mina, not to himself. Ezekiel 45:12 The shekel shall be twenty gerahs; twenty shekels plus twenty-five shekels plus fifteen shekels shall be your mina. Ezekiel sets fixed, honest standards: here a mina of sixty shekels.

Denarius The denarius was a Roman silver coin, the usual day’s wage for a labourer in Jesus’ time. What it was. The denarius (plural denarii) was the standard silver coin of the Roman Empire, weighing about 1/8 oz (3.8 g). It carried the head of the emperor and a title calling him divine or the son of a god, which troubled devout Jews. It is the most common coin in the Gospels; older English Bibles call it a “penny”. In today’s terms. The parable of the vineyard shows that a denarius was a fair day’s pay for a farm labourer. So a good way to think of it is a day’s wage for an unskilled worker today, perhaps £80 to £100 ($100 to $130). Prices then were very different from ours, so this is a guide to buying power rather than an exact exchange rate. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Thinking “a day’s wage” brings many passages alive. Three hundred denarii of ointment was about a year’s income poured out on Jesus. When Jesus was asked about taxes, he asked whose image was on a denarius: coins bearing Caesar’s image belong to Caesar, but we, who bear God’s image, belong wholly to God. In the vineyard parable every worker gets a denarius, whether he worked twelve hours or one, a picture of grace. Matthew 20:2 After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. A denarius was the normal daily wage for a labourer. Matthew 22:19 Show me the coin for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. The coin bore Caesar’s image, which set up Jesus’ answer about what belongs to God. Mark 14:5 For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. The ointment was worth about a year’s wages, a costly act of love for Jesus.

Drachma The drachma was a Greek silver coin worth about the same as a Roman denarius, a day’s wage. What it was. The drachma was the main silver coin of the Greek world, still widely used in the eastern Roman Empire in Jesus’ day. It was roughly equal in value to the denarius. Larger coins were multiples of it: the didrachma (two drachmas) and the tetradrachma or stater (four drachmas). The “ten silver coins” of the woman in Jesus’ parable were drachmas. In today’s terms. Like the denarius, a drachma was worth about a day’s wages for a labourer. Ten drachmas were about ten days’ pay, possibly the woman’s whole savings, perhaps even part of a dowry worn on a headdress, though this is not certain. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Seeing the drachma as a day’s wage makes the lost coin parable easier to feel. The woman is poor, and losing one coin is serious; so she lights a lamp and sweeps the whole dark house until she finds it, then calls her friends to rejoice. Jesus says there is the same joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents. God seeks the lost with that kind of care, and in Christ he comes to find them. Luke 15:8 Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? The coins were drachmas, each about a day’s wage, so the loss mattered greatly. Matthew 17:24 When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax went up to Peter The temple tax of half a shekel was paid with a two-drachma coin.

Lepton and quadrans The lepton was the smallest Jewish copper coin; two of them made a Roman quadrans, the coin of the widow’s offering. What it was. A lepton (plural lepta, “small” or “thin”) was a tiny bronze coin minted in Judea, often called the “widow’s mite” in older English. Two lepta made one quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, which ESV translates “penny”. The money scale ran: a denarius was worth sixteen asses (an “as” or assarion was another small coin), and an as was worth four quadrans. So a lepton was about 1/128 of a denarius. In today’s terms. If a denarius was a day’s wage, a lepton was worth what a labourer earned in about five minutes. Two lepta together were roughly a modern coin you would barely stoop to pick up. Two sparrows were sold for an assarion, which was worth eight lepta. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus watched rich people giving large sums, then praised a poor widow who put in two lepta, “all she had to live on”. God does not measure gifts by size but by the heart and the cost to the giver. “The last penny” in Jesus’ warnings is a quadrans or a lepton: nothing is left unpaid. And God who notices sparrows sold so cheaply notices each of his children. Mark 12:42 And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. Two lepta made one quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. Mark 12:44 For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on. Jesus measures giving by what it costs, not by its size. Luke 12:59 I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny. The “very last penny” is a lepton: the debt must be paid in full.

Stater and the temple tax The stater was a silver coin worth four drachmas, exactly enough to pay the temple tax for two men. What it was. God’s law required every Israelite man counted in the census to give half a shekel “to make atonement” for his life, the same for rich and poor. By Jesus’ day this had become a yearly tax for the upkeep of the temple, collected from Jewish men everywhere. Half a shekel equalled two drachmas, so it was called the “two-drachma tax”. The stater (also called a tetradrachma) was worth four drachmas, the tax for two people. ESV calls the coin in the fish’s mouth “a shekel”, since a stater was the same value as a shekel. In today’s terms. The temple tax of two drachmas was about two days’ wages for a labourer each year. A stater was about four days’ wages. Why it matters when you read the Bible. When the collectors asked Peter whether his teacher paid, Jesus pointed out that kings do not tax their own sons. He is the Son of the One whose house the temple is, so he was free. Yet, to avoid needless offence, he provided a stater for himself and Peter. The half-shekel was atonement money; the Son who owed nothing would soon give himself as the true ransom for many. Exodus 30:15 The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD’s offering to make atonement for your lives. Every life needed the same ransom, whatever a person’s wealth. Matthew 17:26 Then the sons are free. As the Son of God, Jesus owed no tax for his Father’s house. Matthew 17:27 when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself. The coin, a stater, paid the two-drachma tax for two people exactly.

Wages and the value of money The prices and wages mentioned in the Bible show what money could buy and how ordinary people lived. What it was. In New Testament times a labourer earned about a denarius a day, if he found work at all. Many lived from day to day, so the law told employers to pay wages before sunset. Two denarii could pay an innkeeper for a wounded man’s care for some days. Sparrows, the poor man’s meat, sold at two for an assarion (1/16 of a denarius). In famine, prices shot up: Revelation pictures a whole day’s wage buying just one quart of wheat, perhaps eight to sixteen times the normal price. In today’s terms. A simple rule of thumb: take a denarius or a drachma as a day’s pay for an unskilled worker today. Then two hundred denarii is about eight months’ wages; three hundred is about a year’s; a talent is about twenty years’. These are approximate, but they give the right sense of scale. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing what money was worth lets you feel the weight of a passage. Philip’s two hundred denarii was over half a year’s pay and still not enough to feed the crowd, yet Jesus fed them with five loaves. The forgiven debtor in Luke 7 owed five hundred denarii, almost two years’ wages. Jesus’ point is plain: the one forgiven much loves much. John 6:7 Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.” Two hundred denarii was over half a year’s wages, and still far too little. Luke 10:35 And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper The Samaritan paid two days’ wages and promised more, generous care for a stranger. Revelation 6:6 A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius A full day’s wage for one day’s bread pictures severe famine.

Cubit The cubit was the basic Hebrew measure of length, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. What it was. The cubit was a measure taken from the human forearm. It was made up of two spans or six handbreadths. Most building measurements in the Bible are given in cubits: Noah’s ark, the tabernacle and its furniture, Solomon’s temple. There was also a longer “royal” cubit, a cubit plus a handbreadth, which Ezekiel’s temple vision uses. In today’s terms. The common cubit was about 18 in (45 cm); the long cubit about 20½ in (52 cm). So Noah’s ark, 300 by 50 by 30 cubits, was roughly 450 ft long, 75 ft wide and 45 ft high (137 by 23 by 14 m), longer than a football pitch. The ark of the covenant was about 3¾ ft by 2¼ ft by 2¼ ft (1.1 by 0.7 by 0.7 m). Goliath, “six cubits and a span”, was about 9 ft 9 in (nearly 3 m) tall. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Turning cubits into feet and metres helps you picture the scene: the ark was a vast, seaworthy vessel, while the ark of the covenant was a small chest. Precise measurements also remind us that God’s house was built exactly as he directed, a copy of heavenly things, fulfilled in Christ, in whom God dwells among us. Genesis 6:15 the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. The ark was about 450 ft (137 m) long, a huge ship. Exodus 25:10 Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. The ark of the covenant was a chest about 3¾ ft (1.1 m) long. 1 Samuel 17:4 a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span. Goliath was about 9 ft 9 in (nearly 3 m) tall.

Span and handbreadth The span and the handbreadth were small measures of length taken from the human hand. What it was. A span was the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger with the hand spread wide; two spans made a cubit. A handbreadth was the width of the hand across the four fingers at their base; six handbreadths made a cubit. A still smaller unit was the finger’s breadth. These measures were used for small things such as the high priest’s breastpiece, a rim around the table of the bread of the presence, or the thickness of the bronze sea. In today’s terms. A span was about 9 in (23 cm). A handbreadth was about 3 in (7.5 cm), the width of four fingers. You can measure both with your own hand. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because these were everyday measures from a person’s own hand, the Bible uses them for vivid pictures. Isaiah says God marks off the heavens with a span: the whole sky is to him what nine inches is to us. David says his days are only a few handbreadths, a life you could measure across your palm. Our smallness and his greatness drive us to trust him, the eternal God who in Christ gives life that does not end. Isaiah 40:12 Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span The vast heavens are only a hand’s width to God. Psalm 39:5 Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. A whole human life measured in a few hand widths. Exodus 28:16 It shall be square and doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth. The high priest’s breastpiece was about 9 in (23 cm) square.

Reed (measuring rod) The reed was a measuring rod of six long cubits, used for surveying buildings and land. What it was. Reeds grew tall and straight along rivers, so a cut reed made a handy measuring stick. As a unit, Ezekiel’s “measuring reed” was six long cubits, each a cubit and a handbreadth. In visions, an angelic figure with a measuring reed or rod measures the temple and the city of God. In Revelation the reed (Greek kalamos) is a measuring rod like a staff, and once a golden one. In today’s terms. Six long cubits was about 10 ft 4 in (3.1 m), roughly the height of a single-storey room. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Scripture, measuring something marks it out as God’s possession, laid out according to his plan and under his protection. Ezekiel’s exiles, with the temple in ruins, were shown it measured again in exact detail: God had not given up his dwelling with his people. In Revelation John measures the temple and the worshippers, a sign that God keeps his people safe in the midst of trouble. The measured city is the bride of the Lamb. Ezekiel 40:5 the length of the measuring reed in the man’s hand was six long cubits, each being a cubit and a handbreadth in length. A reed was about 10 ft 4 in (3.1 m). Revelation 11:1 Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, Measuring the worshippers marks them as God’s own, kept safe by him.

Stadion (furlong) and mile The stadion was a Greek measure of distance of about 600 ft; the Roman mile was eight stadia. What it was. The stadion (plural stadia) was 600 Greek feet, the length of a running track; our word “stadium” comes from it. Older English Bibles translate it “furlong”, and ESV often turns it into miles or yards in the text. The Roman mile was a thousand paces, about eight stadia. Roman soldiers had the right to force a local man to carry their gear for a mile. In today’s terms. A stadion was about 607 ft (185 m), close to an English furlong of 660 ft (201 m). The Roman mile was about 1,620 yd (1,480 m), slightly shorter than a modern mile. Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem, was about seven miles (11 km), a two or three hour walk. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The holy city in Revelation measures 12,000 stadia each way, about 1,400 miles (2,200 km), a perfect cube larger than any city on earth. Twelve thousand is twelve times a thousand: a city vast enough for the whole people of God, shaped like the Most Holy Place. And Jesus’ command to go a second mile turned a hated duty into an opportunity for unlooked-for kindness. Revelation 21:16 And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. The city is a vast cube, like the Most Holy Place, where God dwells with his people. Matthew 5:41 And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Jesus has in mind the Roman soldier’s right to make a local carry his load for a mile. Luke 24:13 That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, The Greek says sixty stadia, about seven miles (11 km).

A Sabbath day’s journey A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance Jewish teachers allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath. What it was. The law told Israel not to go out to gather manna on the seventh day, “let no one go out of his place”. Later Jewish teachers fixed how far a person might walk without breaking the Sabbath. They set it at two thousand cubits, drawing on the distance kept between the people and the ark when Israel crossed the Jordan and the pasture lands around the Levites’ towns. The phrase appears in the Bible only once, in Acts. In today’s terms. Two thousand cubits is about 1,000 yd (900 m), a little over half a mile, a walk of perhaps fifteen minutes. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Luke uses the phrase to tell us how near the Mount of Olives was to Jerusalem: Jesus ascended from a spot close enough for a short walk home. The rule itself shows how the rabbis built fences around God’s law. Jesus did not set aside the Sabbath, but taught that it was made for man’s good and that he is Lord of it. True Sabbath rest is found in him. Acts 1:12 Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. The Mount of Olives was a little over half a mile (about 900 m) from the city. Exodus 16:29 Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day. Later teachers built the Sabbath day’s journey on this command.

Ephah The ephah was the standard Hebrew dry measure, used for grain and flour. What it was. The ephah was a measure of volume for dry goods. It was equal to the bath, the liquid measure, and was one tenth of a homer. Smaller measures were the seah (a third of an ephah) and the omer (a tenth). The word also meant the container or basket used to measure it. Grain offerings were often a tenth of an ephah of fine flour. In today’s terms. Scholars differ on its size; the commonest estimate is about 5 gallons (22 litres), roughly half a bushel. Some put it lower. An ephah of barley weighs perhaps 30 lb (13 kg). Ruth gleaned about that much in one day. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing an ephah was a large amount shows Boaz’s quiet kindness to Ruth: he made sure she gathered far more than a poor gleaner could expect. The prophets attacked traders who made “the ephah small”, cheating the poor by short measure. God demands a just ephah because he is just. Ruth’s ephah of barley is a small sign of the redeemer’s generosity, which overflows in Christ. Ruth 2:17 So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley. About 30 lb (13 kg) of grain in one day showed Boaz’s generosity. Amos 8:5 that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances, Cheats sold short measure and weighed payments with heavy weights. Exodus 16:36 (An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.) The ephah was the base for smaller measures.

Homer and kor (cor) The homer and the kor were the largest Hebrew measures of volume, each equal to ten ephahs. What it was. The homer was a dry measure of ten ephahs. Its name probably comes from the Hebrew for “donkey”: it was a donkey-load. The kor (or cor) was the same size and was used for both grain and oil. Do not confuse the homer with the omer, which was a hundredth of a homer. A lethech, mentioned once, was probably half a homer. In today’s terms. If an ephah was about 22 litres, a homer or kor was about 220 litres (58 gallons), roughly six bushels, a weight of grain that would load a donkey. Solomon’s court used thirty cors of fine flour a day, about 6,600 litres (1,450 gallons). Why it matters when you read the Bible. Isaiah warned that ten acres of vineyard would give only one bath of wine and a homer of seed only an ephah: sowing ten and reaping one, a picture of God’s judgment on fruitless Israel. Hosea bought back his unfaithful wife for fifteen shekels and a homer and a lethech of barley, a modest price that pictures God’s redeeming love for his adulterous people. Christ paid far more to redeem his bride. Ezekiel 45:11 the homer shall be the standard measure. Ezekiel fixes the homer as the standard; the ephah and the bath are a tenth of it. Isaiah 5:10 For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah. Reaping a tenth of what was sown pictures judgment. Hosea 3:2 So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. Hosea’s purchase pictures God buying back his unfaithful people.

Seah The seah was a Hebrew dry measure, a third of an ephah, used for flour and grain. What it was. The seah was a common household measure. Three seahs made one ephah. Abraham told Sarah to bake with three seahs of fine flour for his visitors, and Elisha promised that a seah of flour would sell for a shekel the next day. In the New Testament, the “three measures” of flour in the parable of the leaven are three seahs (Greek sata). In today’s terms. If an ephah was about 22 litres, a seah was about 7 litres, or about 12 pints, roughly 1½ gallons. Three seahs of flour is about 25 lb (12 kg), enough bread for perhaps a hundred people. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Seeing the size of three seahs shows the lavish hospitality of Abraham, who did not know at first that he was serving the Lord. In Jesus’ parable, a little leaven hidden in that great mass of dough works through it all: so the kingdom of heaven begins small and hidden, yet grows until it fills the world. Elisha’s seah for a shekel was a promise of sudden plenty in a starving city, and it came true exactly as God said. Genesis 18:6 Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes. Abraham prepared a huge amount, about 25 lb (12 kg) of flour. Matthew 13:33 The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened. The three measures are three seahs, a large batch of dough. 2 Kings 7:1 Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria. God promised sudden plenty to a city in famine.

Bath and hin The bath and the hin were Hebrew measures of liquid, used for wine, oil and water. What it was. The bath was the main liquid measure, the same size as the ephah for dry goods: a tenth of a homer or kor. The hin was a smaller measure, a sixth of a bath. Drink offerings and the oil mixed with grain offerings were often measured in parts of a hin. The bronze sea in Solomon’s temple held two thousand baths. In the New Testament the “measures of oil” in Luke 16 are baths, and the stone jars at Cana held two or three Greek measures each. In today’s terms. A bath was about 22 litres (about 5 imperial or 6 US gallons), roughly a large bucket. A hin was about 6½ pints (3.7 litres). A quarter of a hin, the drink offering with a lamb, was about 1½ pints (nearly a litre). Why it matters when you read the Bible. Ezekiel, acting out the siege of Jerusalem, was allowed to drink just a sixth of a hin of water a day, little more than a pint (0.6 litres): a picture of terrible want. In contrast, at Cana Jesus turned 120 to 180 gallons of water into fine wine, a sign of the overflowing joy of the messianic feast he brings. Exodus 29:40 a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine for a drink offering. Daily offerings used measured amounts of oil and wine, about a litre each. Ezekiel 4:11 And water you shall drink by measure, the sixth part of a hin; from day to day you shall drink. A daily water ration of about a pint pictured the siege. John 2:6 Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus’ first sign provided wine in abundance.

Omer The omer was a small Hebrew dry measure, a tenth of an ephah, best known as the daily portion of manna. What it was. The omer appears in the story of the manna. God told each Israelite to gather an omer a day for each person, and twice as much on the sixth day. Exodus explains that an omer is a tenth of an ephah, which is probably the same as the “tenth measure” of flour in many offerings. An omer of manna was kept before the Lord in a jar, later kept in the ark of the covenant (Hebrews 9:4), so that future generations would see the bread God gave. Do not confuse it with the homer, which was a hundred times larger. In today’s terms. If an ephah was about 22 litres, an omer was about 2 litres, roughly 4 pints or 2 quarts, a generous daily portion. Why it matters when you read the Bible. However much or little anyone gathered, when it was measured each had an omer: God gave exactly enough. Paul quotes this to urge Christians to share with those in need. The jar of manna is a reminder of daily dependence, and Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven, who gives life to the world. Exodus 16:16 Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons An omer of manna was each person’s daily portion. Exodus 16:18 But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. God provided exactly enough for everyone. Exodus 16:32 Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness A kept omer reminded Israel of God’s daily provision.

Gerah and beka The gerah and the beka were the smallest Hebrew weights: a gerah was a twentieth of a shekel and a beka half a shekel. What it was. The gerah was the smallest weight named in the Bible. The word probably means a grain or seed, perhaps a carob bean, used as a natural standard. Twenty gerahs made a shekel “of the sanctuary”. The beka means “split” or “divided”: it was half a shekel. Archaeologists have found small stone weights in Israel inscribed “beka”, and others marked “pim”, about two-thirds of a shekel (1 Samuel 13:21). In today’s terms. A gerah weighed about 1/50 oz (0.6 g), about the weight of a paper clip. A beka weighed about 1/5 oz (5.7 g), roughly the weight of a 20p coin. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The beka was the half shekel every Israelite man gave as atonement money when he was counted, and the silver from it made the sockets on which the tabernacle stood. The holy dwelling of God literally rested on the ransom of his people. The gold ring given to Rebekah weighed a beka. Small units remind us that God cares about exact honesty in small things. Exodus 30:13 half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD. Twenty gerahs made a shekel; half of it was the atonement money. Exodus 38:26 a beka a head (that is, half a shekel, by the shekel of the sanctuary), for everyone who was listed in the records The beka from each man provided silver for the tabernacle. Genesis 24:22 the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel The ring for Rebekah weighed a beka, about 1/5 oz (5.7 g).

Weights and scales (honest balances) Weights and scales were how goods and money were measured in Bible times, and God required them to be honest. What it was. Before coins, and for long after, silver was weighed on a balance: a beam with a pan on each side. The buyer’s silver went in one pan and stone or metal weights in the other. Traders carried their weights in a bag. A dishonest merchant kept two sets, a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling, or used a “false balance” that tipped unfairly. Dry goods were measured in baskets such as the ephah, which could also be made too small. In today’s terms. Imagine a shop whose scales are rigged, or a petrol pump that gives less than it shows: cheating by weights was the ordinary fraud of the ancient world, and it hurt the poor most. Why it matters when you read the Bible. God’s law commanded “just balances, just weights”, and Proverbs calls a false balance “an abomination to the LORD”. Honest trade reflects the character of God. Scales also picture judgment: Belshazzar was “weighed in the balances and found wanting”. On our own we would be found wanting too. The gospel tells us that Christ’s perfect righteousness is counted to all who trust in him. Proverbs 11:1 A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. God cares about honesty in ordinary business. Leviticus 19:36 You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: I am the LORD your God Honest measures were part of living as God’s redeemed people. Daniel 5:27 TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; Scales became a picture of God’s judgment.

Hours of the day The way people in Bible times numbered the hours of daylight, counting from sunrise. What it was. In New Testament times the daylight was divided into twelve hours, counted from sunrise to sunset. So “the first hour” was just after dawn, “the third hour” mid-morning, “the sixth hour” midday and “the ninth hour” mid-afternoon. Because the days are longer in summer than in winter, an “hour” was not a fixed length; it was a twelfth of the daylight. The third, sixth and ninth hours were common points for marking the day, and the ninth hour was a regular time of prayer at the temple. In today’s terms. Taking sunrise as about 6 a.m., the third hour is about 9 a.m., the sixth hour about noon, the ninth hour about 3 p.m. and the eleventh hour about 5 p.m. These are approximate, since people had no clocks and judged time by the sun. Scholars differ on whether John sometimes counts hours another way, which may explain why his Gospel places Pilate’s verdict at “about the sixth hour”. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing the hours lets you follow the Gospels’ timetable of the cross: Jesus was crucified at the third hour (about 9 a.m.), darkness covered the land from the sixth hour to the ninth (noon to 3 p.m.), and he died at the very hour the temple’s afternoon sacrifice and prayers were offered. It also gives force to the parable of workers hired at the eleventh hour, with only an hour of daylight left, who still receive the full day’s pay by grace. Mark 15:25 And it was the third hour when they crucified him. Mark dates the crucifixion to about 9 a.m. Mark 15:33 And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. Three hours of darkness, from about noon to 3 p.m., as Christ bore judgment for sin. Acts 3:1 Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. The ninth hour, about 3 p.m., was a set time of prayer at the temple.

Watches of the night The divisions of the night into shifts for guards and watchmen. What it was. Night was divided into “watches”, the stretches of time a guard stood on duty. In the Old Testament the Israelites seem to have used three watches: the first, the “middle watch” (Judges 7:19) and the “morning watch” (Exodus 14:24). By New Testament times the Roman system of four watches was in common use, and the Gospels speak of “the fourth watch of the night”. Jesus names the four informally as evening, midnight, cockcrow and morning. In today’s terms. With nightfall at about 6 p.m., the four Roman watches ran roughly: first watch 6 to 9 p.m., second 9 p.m. to midnight, third midnight to 3 a.m., and fourth 3 to 6 a.m. The three older Hebrew watches were longer, about four hours each. Think of the shifts of a night nurse or a ship’s crew. Why it matters when you read the Bible. When Jesus came to his disciples on the sea “in the fourth watch”, they had been rowing against the wind for most of the night; he came in the darkest, most exhausted hours before dawn. The watches also shape Jesus’ call to be ready for his return: the master may come at any watch, so servants must stay awake. And the psalmist’s longing, waiting for the Lord “more than watchmen for the morning” (Psalm 130:6), draws on the long night shift of the city guard. Matthew 14:25 And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. Jesus came between about 3 and 6 a.m., after a long night of struggle. Mark 13:35 Therefore stay awake Jesus’ list of evening, midnight, cockcrow and morning follows the four night watches. Psalm 90:4 For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night. A whole age is to God like a few hours’ guard duty.

How days were counted The Bible’s way of reckoning a day from evening to evening, and of counting part of a day as a whole day. What it was. In Israel a day began at sunset and ran to the next sunset, following the pattern of creation: “there was evening and there was morning, the first day.” So the Sabbath began on Friday evening. People also counted inclusively: any part of a day was counted as a day, and the first and last days of a span were both included. “On the third day” meant the day after tomorrow, and “after three days” could mean the same thing. In today’s terms. Inclusive counting is like saying that a guest who arrives on Friday evening and leaves on Sunday morning has stayed “three days”: Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Today we would say two nights. Note too that a Jewish “Friday” began at what we call Thursday sunset. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This explains how Jesus could speak of “three days and three nights” and also of rising “on the third day”. He died on Friday afternoon and rose early on Sunday: Friday, Saturday and Sunday make three days by the reckoning of the time, and “three days and three nights” was a common way of saying the same (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1). There is no contradiction. The pattern of evening then morning is also a gentle picture of the gospel: darkness first, then the light of the resurrection morning. Genesis 1:5 And there was evening and there was morning, the first day. From the first day of creation the day is reckoned evening, then morning. Matthew 12:40 so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. A Jewish idiom for parts of three days, not a full seventy-two hours. 1 Corinthians 15:4 that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, Friday to Sunday, counted inclusively, is the third day.

The Jewish calendar and months The calendar of twelve lunar months by which Israel kept its year and its feasts. What it was. Israel’s months followed the moon: each began with the new moon and lasted 29 or 30 days. Twelve such months make about 354 days, so an extra month was added from time to time (later called a second Adar) to keep the feasts in step with the harvests. At the exodus God made the spring month Abib, later called Nisan, “the first month”. The older names in the Bible include Abib, Ziv, Ethanim and Bul; after the exile the Babylonian names were used: Nisan, Iyyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Ab, Elul, Tishri, Marcheshvan, Chislev, Tebeth, Shebat and Adar. The civil year was also reckoned from Tishri in the autumn. In today’s terms. Each Hebrew month overlaps two of ours. Nisan is roughly March to April, Sivan May to June, Tishri September to October, Chislev November to December, and Adar February to March. That is why Easter, tied to Passover, moves around our calendar. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Months in the Bible are mostly given by number, so knowing that “the first month” is spring and “the seventh month” autumn helps you place events and feasts. More deeply, God began Israel’s year with the month of redemption: the people’s calendar was reset around the Passover, as Christians reckon all history around Christ, our Passover lamb. Exodus 12:2 This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you. God reset Israel’s year around the month of the exodus. Exodus 13:4 Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out. Abib, meaning ear of grain, is the old name for the spring month later called Nisan. Esther 3:7 In the first month, which is the month of Nisan After the exile the Babylonian month names came into use.

The Sabbath The seventh day of the week, set apart by God for rest and worship. What it was. The word Sabbath comes from a Hebrew word meaning to stop or rest. God rested on the seventh day of creation and blessed it, and in the Ten Commandments he told Israel to keep it holy, doing no ordinary work. It ran from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. It was a day for rest, worship and the reading of Scripture, and a sign of God’s covenant with Israel. By Jesus’ time the rabbis had added many detailed rules, such as how far one might walk. In today’s terms. Picture the whole land shutting down for a day each week: no shops, no fieldwork, no business, the household and even servants and animals at rest. A “Sabbath day’s journey” (Acts 1:12) was about two thirds of a mile (about 1 km), a limit set by tradition rather than by the law. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Many of Jesus’ clashes with the Pharisees were about the Sabbath. He did not abolish it but showed its true purpose: it was made for man, for rest and mercy, and he is its Lord. The Sabbath points beyond itself to the rest we find in Christ, who finished his work. Reformed churches have generally held, with the Westminster Confession, that the day of rest now continues as the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of his resurrection. Exodus 20:8 Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. The fourth commandment sets the seventh day apart. Mark 2:27 The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Jesus restores the Sabbath as a gift, not a burden. Hebrews 4:9 So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, The weekly rest points to the final rest won by Christ.

The week The cycle of seven days, rooted in God’s six days of work and one of rest at creation. What it was. The seven-day week comes from creation itself: God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Unlike the day, month and year, it is not tied to the sun or moon. The Hebrews did not name their weekdays; they numbered them (“the first day of the week”), and only the seventh had a name, the Sabbath. The sixth day, Friday, came to be called “the day of Preparation”, when food was made ready for the Sabbath. In today’s terms. Our Sunday is “the first day of the week”, Friday is the Preparation, and Saturday is the Sabbath. Jesus’ phrase about the Pharisee who fasts “twice a week” (Luke 18:12) refers to the custom of fasting on Mondays and Thursdays. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Seeing how the week works makes the Passion narrative clear: Jesus died on the day of Preparation, lay in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of the week. That is why the first Christians gathered on the first day, which John calls “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). The ordinary rhythm of seven days still preaches that our time belongs to God, who made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Genesis 2:3 So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation. The week is rooted in the creation week. Acts 20:7 On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread The early church met on Sunday, the day of the resurrection.

Sabbath year Every seventh year, when Israel’s fields were left unsown and debts were released. What it was. God commanded that every seventh year the land itself should have a Sabbath. Fields were not sown and vineyards not pruned; whatever grew by itself was free for the poor, the stranger and the animals. In that year debts between Israelites were to be released (Deuteronomy 15), and the law was read aloud to all the people at the Feast of Booths. God promised enough harvest in the sixth year to carry them through. In today’s terms. Imagine a whole nation of farmers taking a year off every seven years, with no income from new crops, and trusting God for food. It was rather like a fallow field in crop rotation, but done in faith and on a national scale, with debts written off as well. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Israel often failed to keep these years. The Chronicler sees the seventy years of exile as the land at last enjoying the Sabbaths it had been denied. The Sabbath year teaches that the land belonged to the Lord and that his people lived by his provision, not by their own unbroken labour. Its release of debts is a picture of the greater release Christ brings, the forgiveness of our debts before God. Leviticus 25:4 but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. The land itself was to rest every seventh year. Deuteronomy 15:1 At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release. The Sabbath year brought release of debts. 2 Chronicles 36:21 until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years. The exile is linked to Israel’s neglect of the Sabbath years.

Year of Jubilee The fiftieth year, when family land was returned and Israelite servants were set free. What it was. After seven Sabbath years (forty-nine years), the fiftieth year was to be a jubilee. It was announced with a ram’s horn trumpet on the Day of Atonement. Land that a family had sold through poverty went back to them, and Israelites who had sold themselves into service went free. Land was really leased, not sold for ever, and its price depended on how many years remained until the jubilee. The name probably comes from the Hebrew word for the ram’s horn. In today’s terms. It was like a national reset button every fifty years, about once in a lifetime: debts of land cancelled, families restored to their inheritance, and no one held in poverty for ever. Scholars are unsure how fully Israel actually kept it; the Bible does not record a jubilee being celebrated. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The jubilee lies behind Isaiah 61, which Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and declared fulfilled in himself. He came to proclaim “liberty to the captives” and “the year of the Lord’s favor”. The jubilee was proclaimed on the Day of Atonement: freedom follows atonement. So it is with Christ, whose sacrifice brings the true release and restores us to our inheritance as God’s children. Leviticus 25:10 And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you Liberty and return to family land marked the jubilee. Luke 4:18 He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives Jesus takes up jubilee language to describe his mission. Luke 4:19 to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor. The year of the Lord’s favour arrives in Christ.

New moon The first day of each month, marked in Israel with trumpets and offerings. What it was. Because Israel’s months followed the moon, a month began when the thin crescent of the new moon was first seen after sunset. The day was a small holy day: trumpets were blown, extra burnt offerings were made (Numbers 28:11 to 15), and in some periods ordinary trade stopped (Amos 8:5). Families might hold a feast, as Saul did at court, and people sometimes visited a prophet on that day (2 Kings 4:23). The new moon of the seventh month was the Feast of Trumpets. In today’s terms. Think of a monthly holiday that falls on a different date each month by our calendar, set not by a printed diary but by watchers looking for the first sliver of moon in the western sky. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The new moon often appears alongside the Sabbaths and feasts in the Prophets, sometimes in warning when worship had become empty (Isaiah 1:13 to 14). Paul says Christians must not let anyone judge them over a new moon or Sabbath, because these were shadows; the substance is Christ. Yet Isaiah’s vision of the new creation still pictures all flesh coming to worship “from new moon to new moon” (Isaiah 66:23). Numbers 10:10 and at the beginnings of your months, you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings The new moon was marked with trumpets and offerings. Colossians 2:16 Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. Believers are not bound by the old calendar of holy days. Colossians 2:17 These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ. The festivals were shadows; Christ is the reality.

Regnal years The ancient way of dating events by the year of a king’s reign. What it was. There was no universal numbering of years, such as AD, in Bible times. Events were dated by the reign of a king: “in the fourth year of Solomon”, “in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar”, or simply “in the year that King Uzziah died”. Nations differed in how they counted: some called the part-year when a king came to the throne his first year, others counted from the next new year. Kings sometimes also reigned alongside their fathers for a time (a co-regency, meaning a shared reign). In today’s terms. It is like dating something “in the third year of the late Queen’s reign” rather than giving a calendar year. Scholars use these regnal years, together with records from Assyria and Babylon, to fix Bible dates; for example, Solomon’s fourth year, when he began the temple, is usually placed about 966 BC, and the fifteenth year of Tiberius about AD 28 or 29. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Regnal dates anchor the Bible in real history: Luke deliberately sets John the Baptist’s ministry among named rulers. Knowing how kings were counted also explains why the numbers in Kings and Chronicles can look at first as if they do not add up; differences in counting and overlapping reigns usually account for them. And Isaiah’s great vision comes in the year an earthly king died, when he saw the King who does not die. 1 Kings 6:1 in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. Temple building is dated by Solomon’s regnal year. Luke 3:1 In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea Luke dates the gospel events by Roman and local rulers. Isaiah 6:1 In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up A king’s death dates the prophet’s vision of the eternal King.

Passover The spring feast remembering the night the Lord passed over Israel’s homes in Egypt and set them free. What it was. On the night of the exodus each Israelite household killed a spotless lamb and put its blood on the doorposts. When the Lord struck the firstborn of Egypt, he passed over every house marked with blood. Passover was kept every year on the fourteenth day of the first month, Nisan, at twilight. Families ate roast lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, and later wine and the retelling of the story were part of the meal. In Jesus’ day the lambs were sacrificed at the temple, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. In today’s terms. Passover falls in March or April. The date moves each year on our calendar, which is why Easter, timed by the Passover, moves too. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus chose Passover for his death. At the Last Supper, a Passover meal, he gave the bread and cup new meaning as his body and blood. John the Baptist called him “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), and Paul says plainly that Christ is our Passover lamb. As the blood on the doorposts sheltered Israel from judgment, so Christ’s blood shelters all who trust in him. The Lord’s Supper is the Christian fulfilment of the Passover meal. Exodus 12:13 The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you The lamb’s blood marked those whom judgment passed over. 1 Corinthians 5:7 For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Paul names Christ as the true Passover lamb. Luke 2:41 Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. Faithful families went up to Jerusalem for Passover.

Feast of Unleavened Bread The seven-day feast following Passover, when Israel ate bread made without yeast. What it was. From the fifteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, straight after Passover, Israel ate only unleavened bread, flat bread made without leaven (yeast or sourdough). All leaven was cleared out of the house beforehand. It recalled the haste of the exodus, when there was no time for dough to rise. The first and seventh days were holy days of rest. Because the two feasts ran together, the whole week was often simply called Passover. In today’s terms. Think of a week of crackers or flatbread, after a thorough spring clean of every crumb of yeast from the kitchen. The feast falls in March or April, a week long. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In the Bible leaven often pictures something small that spreads through the whole, especially sin and false teaching (Matthew 16:6). Paul uses the feast to call Christians to holy living: because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, we are to clear out the old leaven of malice and live with sincerity and truth. Our holiness does not earn redemption; it follows it, as Unleavened Bread followed Passover. Leviticus 23:6 And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The feast ran for seven days after Passover. Exodus 23:15 You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days God commanded the feast, seven days of bread without leaven. 1 Corinthians 5:8 Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The feast becomes a picture of the Christian life.

Firstfruits The offering of the first sheaf of the barley harvest, given to God at the time of Unleavened Bread. What it was. When Israel came into the land, they were to bring the first sheaf of their harvest to the priest, who waved it before the Lord “on the day after the Sabbath” during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. This was the barley harvest, the first grain to ripen. Until this sheaf was offered, no one was to eat of the new crop. Giving the first part acknowledged that the whole harvest came from God and belonged to him, and it was a pledge that the rest would follow. (Jews have differed over which “Sabbath” is meant.) In today’s terms. It is like giving the very first pay packet of a new job to God before spending any of it. It fell in March or April, about seven weeks before the wheat harvest. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, very probably the day the firstfruits were waved. Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep”. His resurrection is the first sheaf of the great harvest: because he has been raised, all who belong to him will be raised too. The term also describes believers as God’s firstfruits (James 1:18). Leviticus 23:10 you shall bring the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest, The first sheaf was presented to the Lord. 1 Corinthians 15:20 But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Christ’s resurrection guarantees the harvest of his people’s resurrection.

Pentecost (Feast of Weeks) The harvest feast held fifty days after Firstfruits, when the Holy Spirit was poured out on the church. What it was. Seven weeks were counted from the offering of the barley sheaf, and on the fiftieth day came the Feast of Weeks. Pentecost is the Greek name, meaning fiftieth. It celebrated the end of the wheat harvest, and two loaves of bread baked with leaven were offered, along with sacrifices. It was one of the three pilgrim feasts, and in later Jewish tradition it was also linked with the giving of the law at Sinai. In today’s terms. It fell in May or June, a one-day festival at the height of the grain harvest. In the church calendar Pentecost is still kept seven weeks after Easter. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Fifty days after Christ rose, the firstfruits, the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost while Jerusalem was full of pilgrims from many nations. About three thousand were converted that day: the first great harvest of the gospel. Where the law was written on stone, the Spirit now writes it on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3). The feast that once gave thanks for grain now marks the gathering of a people from every nation. Leviticus 23:16 You shall count fifty days to the day after the seventh Sabbath. Then you shall present a grain offering of new grain to the LORD. Pentecost came fifty days after the firstfruits. Deuteronomy 16:16 at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. The Feast of Weeks was one of the three pilgrim feasts. Acts 2:1 When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. The Spirit was poured out on this harvest feast.

Feast of Trumpets The holy day on the first of the seventh month, proclaimed with the blowing of trumpets. What it was. On the first day of the seventh month (Tishri), Israel kept a day of solemn rest, a holy assembly announced by the blowing of trumpets, probably the ram’s horn or shofar. Extra sacrifices were offered (Numbers 29:1 to 6). The Bible says little more about its meaning, but it opened the most solemn month of Israel’s year, calling the people to prepare for the Day of Atonement ten days later and the Feast of Booths after that. In later Judaism it became Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, since the civil year was reckoned from Tishri. In today’s terms. It falls in September or October. A ram’s horn trumpet gives a loud, piercing blast, rather like a call to attention ringing out across a whole city. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Scripture trumpets summon God’s people, announce his presence, sound alarm and herald a king. Here they called Israel to stop, remember the Lord and prepare to meet him. The New Testament speaks of the last trumpet at Christ’s return, when the dead will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The feast reminds us to be ready for the day when the Lord comes. Leviticus 23:24 In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe a day of solemn rest, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation. The feast opened the solemn seventh month. Joel 2:1 Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain! The trumpet calls God’s people to attention before his coming.

Day of Atonement Israel’s most solemn day, when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for the nation’s sins. What it was. On the tenth day of the seventh month the whole nation fasted and rested. Only on this day the high priest, having first offered for his own sins, went behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place with the blood of a bull and of a goat, and sprinkled it on the mercy seat (the lid of the ark). Then he laid his hands on a second goat, the scapegoat, confessed over it the sins of Israel, and sent it away into the wilderness. Atonement means the covering and removing of sin so that people are made right with God. In Hebrew it is Yom Kippur; Acts 27:9 calls it simply “the Fast”. In today’s terms. It falls in September or October, a day of fasting from sunset to sunset, still the holiest day of the Jewish year. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The letter to the Hebrews explains the Day of Atonement as a picture of Christ. The high priest went in once a year, again and again, with the blood of animals; Christ, our great High Priest, entered God’s presence once for all with his own blood. He is both the sacrifice that pays for sin and the scapegoat that carries it away. And at his death the temple curtain was torn in two, opening the way to God. Leviticus 16:30 For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. The day promised cleansing from all Israel’s sins. Leviticus 16:21 And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel The scapegoat bore the people’s sins away. Hebrews 9:12 he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption. Christ fulfils the Day of Atonement once for all.

Feast of Tabernacles (Booths) The joyful autumn harvest feast when Israel lived in shelters made of branches. What it was. From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, for seven days with an eighth day of assembly, Israel lived in booths, or tabernacles: simple shelters of branches and leaves. This recalled the wilderness years, when God cared for his people living in tents. It also gave thanks for the gathering of the grape and olive harvest at the end of the year, so it was the most joyful of the feasts. It was one of the three pilgrim feasts. By Jesus’ time, Jewish sources describe priests pouring out water at the altar each day, and great lamps lighting up the temple courts. In today’s terms. It falls in September or October. Picture a week-long harvest festival where families camp out in leafy shelters on rooftops and in courtyards. Why it matters when you read the Bible. John 7 and 8 are set at this feast. On the last great day, as water was poured out, Jesus cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”, promising the Spirit; soon after he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). John also writes that the Word “dwelt”, literally tabernacled, among us (John 1:14). Zechariah 14:16 foresees the nations keeping this feast, a picture of the final harvest when God dwells with his people. Leviticus 23:42 You shall dwell in booths for seven days. The people lived in shelters for the week. Leviticus 23:43 that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt The booths recalled God’s care in the wilderness. John 7:37 On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Jesus offers himself as the true source of living water.

Purim The feast celebrating the deliverance of the Jews from Haman’s plot in the days of Esther. What it was. In the Persian Empire, about 474 BC, Haman cast lots (pur, plural purim) to choose a day for destroying the Jews. Through Esther and Mordecai, God overturned the plot, and the Jews were saved. Mordecai and Esther then set the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar as yearly days of feasting and joy, of sending food to one another and gifts to the poor. Purim was not commanded in the law of Moses, but it became a lasting Jewish festival, with the book of Esther read aloud. In today’s terms. It falls in February or March, a cheerful carnival-like celebration, still kept by Jews today with feasting, gifts and the reading of Esther. Why it matters when you read the Bible. God’s name does not appear in Esther, yet the whole story shows his hidden hand ruling over “chance”: the very lots cast to destroy his people gave the feast its name. As Proverbs 16:33 says, the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord. Purim reminds believers that God keeps his promises to preserve his people, and through them the line that led to Christ. Esther 9:26 Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. The feast was named after the lots Haman cast. Esther 9:22 as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday Purim celebrates God turning sorrow into joy.

Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) The winter feast remembering the cleansing and rededication of the temple in 164 BC. What it was. In 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV Epiphanes defiled the temple in Jerusalem, setting up a pagan altar and offering pigs. Judas Maccabeus led a Jewish revolt, and in December 164 BC the temple was cleansed and rededicated to the Lord. An eight-day feast was set up to remember it, beginning on the twenty-fifth of Chislev. It is told in 1 Maccabees, not in the Old Testament, and it was also called the Feast of Lights. Its name, Hanukkah, means dedication. In today’s terms. It falls in late November or December, an eight-day festival of lamps and lights, still kept by Jews today. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The only mention in the Bible is John 10:22, where Jesus walks in the temple at this feast. As the Jews remembered the temple made holy again, Jesus, who is himself the true temple (John 2:19 to 21), spoke of being the one “whom the Father consecrated” (John 10:36), the same idea as dedication, and declared, “I and the Father are one.” The prophecies of Daniel 8 and 11 are commonly understood to foresee the events behind this feast. John 10:22 At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, The feast is mentioned only here in the Bible. John 10:23 and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon. Jesus, the true temple, is present at the feast of the temple.

Pilgrim feasts The three yearly feasts for which Israelite men went up to worship at Jerusalem. What it was. God commanded every Israelite man to appear before him three times a year at the place he would choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread (with Passover), at the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) and at the Feast of Booths. Once the temple was built, that place was Jerusalem. Whole families often travelled together in large groups, as Jesus’ family did. Because Jerusalem stands high in the hills, people always spoke of going “up” to it. Psalms 120 to 134, the “Songs of Ascents”, were probably sung by pilgrims on the way. In today’s terms. Think of hundreds of thousands of people converging on one city for a festival, walking for days. From Nazareth to Jerusalem is about 70 to 80 miles (110 to 130 km), several days on foot. Jews scattered through the empire also came, as at Pentecost in Acts 2. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Many Gospel events happen at these feasts, especially in John, where Jesus goes up to Jerusalem again and again, and finally goes up to die at Passover. Knowing the pilgrim feasts explains the crowds, the excitement and the danger. The songs of the pilgrims express the joy of drawing near to God, which in Christ is now open to all, wherever they are (John 4:21 to 24; Hebrews 12:22). Deuteronomy 16:16 Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose God appointed three pilgrim feasts each year. Luke 2:41 Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. Jesus grew up in a family that made the pilgrimage. Psalm 122:1 I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD!” A pilgrim song of joy in going up to worship.

Pharisees A Jewish movement of devout laymen in Jesus’ day, devoted to keeping God’s law and the traditions built around it. What it was. The Pharisees were probably named from a word meaning “separated ones”. They grew up in the two centuries before Christ and became the most respected religious party among ordinary Jews. Most were not priests but laymen who met in fellowship groups. They believed in the resurrection, angels and God’s rule over history, and they held that the written law of Moses came with an “oral law”, the “tradition of the elders”, which spelled out how to keep it in daily life: washing, tithing, Sabbath rules and food. In today’s terms. The historian Josephus, writing late in the first century, put their number at about 6,000. Think of a small, serious, highly respected renewal movement whose members set the standard of godliness in every town. When people thought of a truly religious man, they thought of a Pharisee. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because the Pharisees were the most admired people of their day, Jesus’ words that our righteousness must exceed theirs (Matthew 5:20) were shocking. The danger he exposed was not love of the law but trusting in law-keeping, adding human rules to God’s word, and despising sinners. Not all Pharisees opposed him: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came to faith, and Paul, a Pharisee, learned to count his own righteousness as loss in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:4-9). Luke 18:11 The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable trusts in his own goodness and looks down on others; it is the tax collector who goes home justified. Philippians 3:5 circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; Paul lists being a Pharisee among the advantages he gave up as loss for the sake of Christ. Pharisaism is not only a first-century problem: every heart is tempted to rest on its own record instead of on Christ.

Sadducees A small, wealthy party linked to the high priests and the temple, who denied the resurrection. What it was. The Sadducees were the party of the priestly aristocracy in Jerusalem, closely tied to the temple and to the high-priestly families. Their name probably comes from Zadok, the high priest in Solomon’s day. They rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and held to the written law; scholars differ on whether they gave the prophets and other writings less weight. They denied the resurrection of the body, angels and spirits, and they were content to cooperate with Rome to keep the temple running and their own position secure. In today’s terms. Picture a small establishment of powerful families: few in number, rich, politically careful, and in charge of the nation’s central institution. They had little following among the common people. When the temple was destroyed in AD 70 their power base vanished, and they disappear from history. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing who the Sadducees were explains why they tried to trap Jesus with a riddle about a woman married seven times (Matthew 22:23-33): they thought the resurrection was absurd. Jesus answered from the books of Moses they accepted, showing that God is “the God of the living”. It also explains why the apostles’ preaching of Jesus’ resurrection so angered the high priest and “the party of the Sadducees” (Acts 5:17), and how Paul could divide the council by declaring his hope in the resurrection (Acts 23:6-8). Matthew 22:23 The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, Their denial of the resurrection lies behind their question to Jesus. Acts 23:8 For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Luke explains the main difference between the two parties that sat together in the council.

Scribes (teachers of the law) Experts in the law of Moses who copied, studied, explained and applied it. What it was. In the Old Testament a scribe could simply be a royal secretary, but after the exile the word came to mean a scholar of God’s law. Ezra is the great example: a priest and “a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses” who set his heart to study it, do it and teach it. By the New Testament, scribes (also called “lawyers” and “teachers of the law”) were trained experts who interpreted the Scriptures, taught pupils and gave rulings on legal questions. Many belonged to the Pharisees, and some sat in the Sanhedrin. In today’s terms. They combined the roles of Bible scholar, lawyer and professor. A scribe’s authority rested on quoting earlier teachers: “Rabbi so-and-so says”. That is why people were struck when Jesus said, “But I say to you”. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The crowds were astonished that Jesus taught “as one who had authority, and not as the scribes” (Mark 1:22). He did not lean on the opinions of others; he spoke as the Lord of the law. Jesus warned against scribes who loved honour and devoured widows’ houses (Mark 12:38-40), yet he also praised a scribe who was “not far from the kingdom of God” (Mark 12:34) and spoke of every scribe trained for the kingdom bringing out treasures new and old (Matthew 13:52). Ezra 7:10 For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel. Ezra is the model scribe: studying, obeying and teaching God’s word. Mark 1:22 And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. Jesus’ teaching carried an authority the scribes, who leaned on tradition, did not have.

The Sanhedrin (the council) The supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, which governed the nation’s religious and local affairs under Rome. What it was. The Sanhedrin (from a Greek word for “sitting together”) is usually called simply “the council” in English Bibles. Later Jewish writings say it had seventy-one members, perhaps modelled on the seventy elders of Moses (Numbers 11:16) plus the presiding high priest. It was made up of “the chief priests, the elders and the scribes”, so both Sadducees and Pharisees sat in it. Under Roman rule it judged religious and many civil cases, but it seems it could not carry out a death sentence without the Roman governor (John 18:31). In today’s terms. Think of a supreme court and senate combined, with real power but always under the watchful eye of the Roman governor, who could overrule it. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Sanhedrin tried Jesus at night, looked for false witnesses and condemned him for blasphemy when he declared that he was the Son of Man who would sit at God’s right hand (Mark 14:55-64). Because it could not execute, it handed him to Pilate. In Acts the same council arrested and beat the apostles, and Stephen and Paul stood before it. Yet God had his people even there: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, and Gamaliel, who warned that if this work was of God the council could not overthrow it (Acts 5:34-39). Mark 14:55 Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. The highest court in the land could find no true charge against Jesus. Acts 5:34 But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher, urged the council to caution.

Chief priests and the high priest The high priest was Israel’s chief religious leader; the “chief priests” were the leading priestly families around him. What it was. God appointed Aaron as the first high priest, and the office passed to his descendants. Only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year on the Day of Atonement, to make atonement for the people (Leviticus 16). By Jesus’ day the office had become political: the Romans appointed and removed high priests at will. Annas held the office from AD 6 to 15, and five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (about AD 18 to 36) followed him, so Annas remained the power behind the scenes. “Chief priests” means the serving high priest, former high priests and the heads of the leading priestly families. In today’s terms. Imagine a ruling family that combined the archbishopric, the presidency of the supreme court and control of the nation’s great treasury, holding office at the pleasure of a foreign governor. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The chief priests led the plot against Jesus. Caiaphas said it was better that one man should die for the people than that the nation perish, and John notes that, without meaning to, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation and for God’s scattered children (John 11:49-52). Hebrews shows that Jesus is the true and final High Priest, who offered himself once for all and now lives to intercede for his people. John 11:49-50 But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.” Caiaphas spoke cynical politics, but God made his words a prophecy of substitution. Hebrews 4:14 Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. Every earthly high priest pointed to Jesus, the great High Priest in heaven.

Priests and Levites The tribe of Levi, set apart to serve God at the tabernacle and temple; Aaron’s descendants were the priests. What it was. God chose the tribe of Levi to serve him in place of Israel’s firstborn. Within that tribe, the descendants of Aaron were priests: they offered sacrifices, burned incense, blessed the people and taught the law. The other Levites assisted them: guarding the sanctuary, carrying the tabernacle in the wilderness, and later serving as singers, gatekeepers and helpers in the temple. They received no tribal territory; the Lord was their inheritance, and they lived on the tithes and offerings. David organised the priests into twenty-four divisions that served in turns (1 Chronicles 24). In today’s terms. In Jesus’ day there were thousands of priests, perhaps as many as 7,000 to 8,000 according to some estimates, plus Levites. Each division served in the temple for about a week, twice a year, and at the great feasts. Most of the year an ordinary priest lived at home, like Zechariah, John the Baptist’s father, in the hill country of Judea. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In the parable of the good Samaritan, the priest and Levite who passed by are the very men whose calling was to show God’s mercy, which sharpens the point (Luke 10:31-32). Above all, the priests’ endless sacrifices show why we need Christ: “the former priests were many in number” because they died, but Jesus “holds his priesthood permanently”, and all believers are now a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Numbers 18:6 And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting. The Levites were God’s gift to Aaron’s priestly family for the service of the sanctuary. Luke 10:31-32 Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. Those set apart for God’s service failed to show mercy. Hebrews 7:23-25 The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever.
