Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. Christ’s priesthood surpasses Levi’s because he lives forever to intercede.

Elders Senior men who led and judged among God’s people, in Israel’s towns and later in the churches. What it was. From early times Israel was led by elders: heads of families and clans who judged disputes at the town gate, gave counsel and represented the people. Moses gathered seventy elders to share his burden (Numbers 11:16). In the New Testament, “the elders” are often the lay leaders who sat with the chief priests and scribes in the Sanhedrin, and “the tradition of the elders” means rulings handed down by earlier teachers. In the church, the apostles appointed elders (also called overseers or bishops) to shepherd, teach and guard each congregation (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5-9). In today’s terms. The word is about maturity and respect more than exact age. Think of the trusted senior figures in a community whose wisdom settles quarrels and whose judgment others follow. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing who “the elders” are helps you tell apart the council that condemned Jesus, the traditions he challenged (Mark 7:1-13), and the shepherds he gives to his church. Reformed churches have long seen in the New Testament a plurality of elders in each church, serving under Christ, the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:1-4). Numbers 11:16 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you. God shared Moses’ load of leadership with seventy elders. Mark 7:3 (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, The tradition of the elders shaped Pharisaic practice, such as ritual washing. Acts 14:23 And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in every new church.

Samaritans The people of Samaria, between Judea and Galilee, with a mixed ancestry and a rival form of worship. What it was. After Assyria conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BC, it deported many Israelites and settled foreigners in their place. They intermarried with the Israelites who remained and at first worshipped the Lord alongside their own gods (2 Kings 17:24-41). In later centuries the Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and built a rival temple on Mount Gerizim, which a Jewish ruler destroyed in the second century BC. They opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem in Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s day. By Jesus’ time Jews and Samaritans despised each other, and many Galilean pilgrims went the long way round to avoid Samaria. In today’s terms. Think of two neighbouring communities with a shared family history, centuries of bitter quarrels and a disputed holy site, where calling someone a Samaritan was an insult (John 8:48). A small Samaritan community still survives today near Mount Gerizim. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This is what makes Jesus’ dealings with Samaritans so striking. He chose a Samaritan as the hero of his parable of neighbour-love, spoke with a Samaritan woman at the well and revealed himself as the Messiah, and noted that the only healed leper who returned to give thanks was a Samaritan (Luke 17:16). After Pentecost the gospel reached Samaria (Acts 8), as Jesus had commanded (Acts 1:8). 2 Kings 17:24 And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities. The Assyrian resettlement explains the Samaritans’ mixed origins. John 4:9 The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.) The woman’s surprise shows how deep the hostility ran. Luke 10:33 But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. Jesus made the despised outsider the example of compassion.

Tax collectors Local Jews who collected tolls and taxes for Rome or for the Herods, and were despised as traitors and cheats. What it was. The Romans did not collect most local taxes themselves. They sold the right to collect tolls, customs and other dues to contractors, who hired local men to gather them. Those collectors could charge more than was owed and keep the difference, and many grew rich this way. Because they worked for the occupying power and handled Gentile money, other Jews treated them as unclean and grouped them with “sinners” and prostitutes. Matthew (Levi) worked at a tax booth in Capernaum, on a trade route, collecting for Herod Antipas. Zacchaeus at Jericho was a “chief tax collector”, over others. In today’s terms. Imagine someone who worked for an enemy occupation, set his own rates and was known to line his pockets: a collaborator and a crook in one person. Respectable people would not eat with him. Why it matters when you read the Bible. So when Jesus called Matthew, ate with tax collectors and went to Zacchaeus’ house, he scandalised the religious, and he showed that he came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). True conversion showed in changed lives: John told tax collectors to take no more than authorised, and Zacchaeus restored fourfold. In Jesus’ parable it is the tax collector, pleading “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”, who goes home justified (Luke 18:13-14). Luke 3:12-13 Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” Even tax collectors came to repent, and John called them to honesty. Matthew 9:10-11 And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus’ table fellowship with outcasts offended the Pharisees. Luke 19:8 And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” Zacchaeus’ repentance went beyond what the law required.

Zealots Jews who were zealous for God’s law and ready to use force to free Israel from Roman rule. What it was. “Zealot” comes from a word meaning “zealous”, and it recalled heroes like Phinehas (Numbers 25) and the Maccabees, who fought for God’s honour. In AD 6 Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census, teaching that paying tribute to Caesar was treason against God. His ideas lived on among Jewish freedom fighters. The Zealots as an organised party appear most clearly in the great revolt of AD 66 to 70, which ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple. Scholars differ on how organised the movement was earlier, in Jesus’ day. In today’s terms. Think of an armed resistance movement inspired by religion: patriots in their own eyes, dangerous rebels in Rome’s. Why it matters when you read the Bible. One of the Twelve was “Simon who was called the Zealot” (Luke 6:15), perhaps because of his past politics, perhaps because of his zeal for the law. Among the apostles he sat beside Matthew, a former tax collector: a man who had fought Rome next to a man who had served it, made one in Christ. This also helps explain why Jesus refused to be made a political king (John 6:15) and why the question about paying taxes to Caesar was such a trap (Mark 12:13-17). Acts 5:37 After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. Gamaliel recalls the failed revolt of Judas the Galilean. Luke 6:15 and Simon who was called the Zealot, Jesus called a Zealot to be one of his apostles.

Herodians Jews who supported the rule of Herod’s family, and so, indirectly, Roman rule. What it was. The Herodians are mentioned only a few times in the Gospels, and nothing is known of them outside the New Testament. They were probably supporters and officials of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who wanted the Herod family to keep or extend its power, perhaps even to rule Judea again as Herod the Great once had. They were political rather than religious, and naturally at odds with the Pharisees, who resented foreign influence. In today’s terms. Think of a political faction loyal to a ruling dynasty, more interested in keeping the peace with Rome than in religious reform. Why it matters when you read the Bible. What is remarkable is that the Herodians and the Pharisees, normally rivals, joined forces against Jesus. After he healed on the Sabbath, they plotted together how to destroy him (Mark 3:6), and later they came together with a trick question about paying taxes to Caesar (Mark 12:13-17). If Jesus said “Pay”, he would lose the people; if he said “Do not pay”, the Herodians could report him as a rebel. His answer, to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s, silenced both. Enemies of Christ often find common cause. Mark 3:6 The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. Old rivals united in their opposition to Jesus. Mark 12:13 And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. The two parties set a political and religious trap together.

Essenes (and the Dead Sea Scrolls) A strict Jewish movement of Jesus’ time, probably linked with the community that kept the Dead Sea Scrolls. What it was. The Essenes are not named in the Bible, but Josephus, Philo and the Roman writer Pliny describe them. They lived simply, often held property in common, kept strict rules of purity, and looked for God to act soon to judge the wicked. Many scholars think the community at Qumran, by the Dead Sea, was Essene, though some differ. They saw themselves as preparing “the way of the Lord” in the wilderness, quoting Isaiah 40:3. From 1947 onwards, scrolls were found in caves near Qumran, hidden there probably before the Romans destroyed the site in about AD 68. In today’s terms. The Dead Sea Scrolls include parts of every Old Testament book except Esther. The great Isaiah scroll is about a thousand years older than the oldest Hebrew copies previously known, yet it agrees remarkably with them. It is like finding your family Bible’s great-great-grandparent and seeing that the words have been faithfully handed down. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Essenes help you see the world in which John the Baptist preached in the wilderness, though there is no evidence he was one of them. Above all, the Scrolls give strong evidence that God has preserved the text of the Old Testament with great care, so that the Scriptures we read are the Scriptures Jesus read. Isaiah 40:3 A voice cries: “In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. The Qumran community applied this verse to themselves; the Gospels apply it to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ. Luke 1:80 And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel. John grew up in the wilderness, the same region where the Qumran community lived.

Synagogue A local Jewish meeting house for prayer, reading of the Scriptures and teaching. What it was. “Synagogue” means a gathering, and then the building where people gathered. Synagogues probably began during or after the exile, when the temple was gone or far away. Every Sabbath, Jews met to pray, recite the Shema (“Hear, O Israel”), and hear readings from the Law and the Prophets, followed by an explanation. A “ruler of the synagogue” arranged the services and could invite visitors to speak. The synagogue also served as a school and community centre. Later Jewish tradition says ten men were needed to form one. In today’s terms. Think of a village chapel that was also the school and town hall. Ruins of first-century synagogues have been found in places such as Magdala and Gamla, and the later synagogue at Capernaum stands on earlier foundations, perhaps of the very building where Jesus taught. Why it matters when you read the Bible. It was Jesus’ custom to go to the synagogue on the Sabbath, and there he read Isaiah 61 and announced, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). Paul began his mission in each city at the synagogue, reasoning from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise. The first Christian meetings drew on the same pattern of Scripture reading, prayer and preaching. Luke 4:16 And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. Jesus worshipped faithfully at the synagogue each Sabbath. Acts 15:21 For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” The law of Moses was read every Sabbath in synagogues across the empire. Acts 17:2 And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, Paul’s custom was to begin with the synagogue and the Scriptures.

Proselytes and God-fearers Gentiles drawn to Israel’s God: proselytes became full converts to Judaism; God-fearers worshipped without fully converting. What it was. A proselyte was a Gentile who joined the Jewish people completely. For a man that meant circumcision; for converts it probably also meant a ritual washing and, while the temple stood, an offering. “God-fearers” (sometimes called “devout” or “worshippers of God”) were Gentiles who believed in the one true God, attended the synagogue, prayed and gave to the poor, and kept some of the law, but did not take the full step of circumcision. Many were found in synagogues throughout the Roman world. In today’s terms. Think of people who come regularly to church, love the Bible and pray, but have not yet joined as members. Many Gentiles of the time admired Judaism’s one God and high morals, but circumcision and the food laws were a great barrier. Why it matters when you read the Bible. These groups were often the first to welcome the gospel. Cornelius, “a devout man who feared God”, was the first Gentile to receive the Spirit (Acts 10). Lydia was “a worshipper of God” (Acts 16:14). In Christ they found what they had been seeking: full membership in God’s people, not through circumcision but through faith alone. This is the heart of the debate in Acts 15 and Galatians. Acts 2:10-11 visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Proselytes were among the crowd at Pentecost. Acts 10:2 a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. Cornelius was a God-fearer before he heard the gospel. Acts 13:43 And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. Converts to Judaism were among the first to follow Paul and Barnabas.

Gentiles Everyone who was not a Jew: “the nations” outside God’s covenant people Israel. What it was. The Hebrew and Greek words translated “Gentiles” simply mean “nations” or “peoples”. In the Bible the word usually means all non-Israelites. The law kept Israel distinct from the nations, to guard her from their idols. By the New Testament, strict Jews avoided eating with Gentiles or entering their homes. In Herod’s temple Gentiles could go into the outer “Court of the Gentiles” but no further: a stone barrier carried notices, one of which has been found, warning that any foreigner who went beyond would have himself to blame for his death. In today’s terms. Think of a high wall with a warning sign, dividing the world into insiders and outsiders. Most readers of this commentary are Gentiles by birth, outsiders who have been welcomed in. Why it matters when you read the Bible. From the start God promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed. The prophets foresaw the nations streaming to the Lord. In Christ that promise is fulfilled: he has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), so that Gentiles who were far off are brought near by his blood. Much of Acts, Romans and Galatians makes sense only when you see this great surprise of grace. Genesis 12:3 and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. God’s promise to Abraham had the nations in view from the beginning. Ephesians 2:12-13 remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Gentiles once without hope are brought near through Christ’s blood. Acts 13:48 And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Gentiles rejoiced to hear the gospel and believed.

Rabbi A title of respect meaning “my teacher” or “my master”, used for a recognised teacher of the law. What it was. “Rabbi” comes from a Hebrew word meaning “great”, so it means something like “my great one”, “my master”. In Jesus’ day it was a respectful way of addressing a teacher who had disciples; it was not yet the formal ordained office it later became in Judaism. “Rabboni”, used by Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (John 20:16), is a warmer, stronger form. A rabbi’s disciples followed him, lived with him, learned his teaching by heart and served him. In today’s terms. The nearest English equivalents are “Teacher”, “Master” or “Sir”, as a student might address a respected professor or a pupil his tutor. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The first disciples called Jesus “Rabbi” and asked where he was staying (John 1:38); Nicodemus, himself a teacher, addressed him the same way. But as the Gospels unfold, the disciples learn that he is much more than a rabbi: he is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Lord. Jesus warned his followers not to seek the title for themselves, “for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:8). Christian teachers serve under the one Teacher. John 1:38 Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are you staying?” John explains the word for his Greek-speaking readers. John 3:2 This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.” Nicodemus honoured Jesus as a teacher from God, yet had still to learn he must be born again. Matthew 23:8 But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. Jesus is the one Teacher of his people.

Centurion A Roman army officer commanding a company of soldiers, nominally a hundred. What it was. A centurion (from the Latin for “hundred”) commanded a “century”, which in practice usually numbered about eighty men. Sixty centurions served in a legion of about 5,000. They were experienced professional soldiers, often promoted from the ranks for courage and reliability, and were the backbone of Rome’s army, responsible for discipline, training and leading from the front. Centurions served in auxiliary units too, such as those stationed in Judea and Caesarea. In today’s terms. Think of a seasoned company commander or sergeant-major: a man used to giving orders and having them obeyed. A centurion was paid many times what an ordinary soldier received and was a man of standing in a town. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Every centurion named in the New Testament is shown in a good light. One in Capernaum understood authority so well that he knew Jesus need only speak the word, and Jesus marvelled at his faith. The centurion at the cross, seeing how Jesus died, confessed, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” Cornelius, a centurion, was the first Gentile convert in Acts, and the centurion Julius treated Paul kindly on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:1-3). Christ’s kingdom reached the very men who enforced Rome’s power. Matthew 8:8-10 But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. A soldier’s grasp of authority became a model of faith in Christ’s word. Mark 15:39 And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” The officer in charge of the crucifixion confessed who Jesus was. Acts 10:1 At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, Cornelius, a centurion, opened a new chapter in the spread of the gospel.

Roman citizenship Legal membership of the Roman state, which brought important rights and protection. What it was. Roman citizenship spread gradually beyond Rome itself. In the first century it could come by birth to a citizen father, by grant as a reward for service, on being freed by a citizen master, or (as with the tribune Claudius Lysias) by paying a large sum, perhaps as a bribe to officials. Citizens had the right to a fair trial, could not be flogged or tortured without condemnation, could not be crucified, and could appeal to Caesar. Certain cities, such as Philippi, were Roman colonies whose people were proud citizens. In today’s terms. It was a little like holding the passport of the world’s greatest power: falsely claiming it was punishable by death, so officials took the claim seriously. Probably only a minority of people in the eastern provinces were citizens. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Paul was a citizen by birth, perhaps because his father or grandfather had been granted it. He used his rights wisely, not to escape suffering but to protect the young church and to carry the gospel to Rome: in Philippi he made the magistrates own their wrong, in Jerusalem he escaped flogging, and before Festus he appealed to Caesar. Writing to the proud citizens of Philippi, he reminded them that “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Acts 22:25-28 But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” Paul’s citizenship by birth outranked a citizenship bought with money. Acts 16:37 But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” Paul insisted that the magistrates at Philippi recognise the wrong done to citizens. Philippians 3:20 But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, The Christian’s highest citizenship is in heaven.

Herod the Great The king of Judea under Rome when Jesus was born, a great builder and a ruthless ruler. What it was. Herod was of Idumean (Edomite) descent; his family had been forced to convert to Judaism. Rome named him “king of the Jews” in 40 BC, and he took Jerusalem in 37 BC, ruling until his death in 4 BC. He was a brilliant politician and an extraordinary builder: he rebuilt and enlarged the temple from about 20 BC, and built the harbour city of Caesarea, the fortress of Masada and the Herodium. He was also violently suspicious. He executed his wife Mariamne and three of his own sons, and Augustus is said to have joked that it was safer to be Herod’s pig than his son. In today’s terms. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born before then, probably about 6 to 4 BC. (Our calendar was worked out centuries later and slightly miscalculated.) Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world; its huge retaining walls, including the Western Wall, still stand. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Matthew sets two kings side by side: Herod, the “king of the Jews” appointed by Rome, and the child born “king of the Jews” (Matthew 2:2). Herod’s murder of the boys of Bethlehem fits all we know of his character, and recalls Pharaoh killing Israel’s sons. As Moses was spared, so was Jesus, the greater Moses, and the true King lived while the tyrant died. Matthew 2:1 Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, Jesus was born while Herod was still king. Matthew 2:16 Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. Herod’s jealous cruelty fell on the infants of Bethlehem. Luke 1:5 In the days of Herod, king of Judea, Luke also dates the story to Herod’s reign.

Herod Antipas A son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee and Perea throughout Jesus’ ministry and beheaded John the Baptist. What it was. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, Augustus divided his kingdom. Antipas became tetrarch (a ruler of part of a kingdom) of Galilee and Perea, the regions where Jesus grew up and did much of his ministry. The Gospels call him “Herod” and sometimes “king”. He rebuilt Sepphoris near Nazareth and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee. He divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. John the Baptist condemned this marriage, and Antipas imprisoned him and, at Herodias’ urging, had him beheaded. He ruled until AD 39, when the emperor Caligula banished him. In today’s terms. A tetrarch was like a regional governor with a royal title, ruling by Rome’s permission. Antipas reigned for about 43 years, the whole of Jesus’ life. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Antipas was curious about Jesus yet hard of heart. Jesus called him “that fox”, crafty and destructive (Luke 13:32). When Pilate sent Jesus to him during the trial, Antipas hoped to see a miracle; Jesus gave him not a word, and Herod and his soldiers mocked him (Luke 23:8-12). Both he and Pilate found Jesus guilty of nothing, yet let him die, fulfilling what Psalm 2 foretold of rulers gathered against the Lord’s Anointed (Acts 4:25-28). Mark 6:17-18 For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” John the Baptist rebuked Antipas for taking his brother’s wife. Luke 13:32 And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Jesus would finish his course whatever Herod plotted. Luke 23:11 And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. Antipas mocked Jesus at his trial.

Herod Archelaus A son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea so harshly that Rome removed him after about ten years. What it was. After Herod the Great’s death in 4 BC, Archelaus received the largest share of his kingdom: Judea, Samaria and Idumea, with the title “ethnarch” (ruler of a people) rather than king. He began his reign by having about 3,000 people killed at the temple during Passover, according to Josephus. A delegation of Jews went to Rome to ask Augustus not to let him reign. His rule stayed brutal, and in AD 6 Augustus deposed him and banished him to Gaul. From then on Judea was governed directly by Roman prefects, of whom Pontius Pilate was one. In today’s terms. He held power for about ten years. His removal is the reason Judea had a Roman governor, rather than a Herod, when Jesus was tried. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Archelaus appears by name only once in the Bible, but that verse explains why Jesus grew up in Nazareth: Joseph was afraid to settle in Judea under such a ruler and was directed in a dream to Galilee (Matthew 2:22-23). Many scholars think Jesus’ parable of a nobleman who went to a far country to receive a kingdom, while his citizens sent a delegation saying they did not want him, echoes the events of Archelaus’ accession (Luke 19:12-27). Matthew 2:22 But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. Archelaus’ reputation steered the holy family to Galilee. Luke 19:14 But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ This detail of the parable probably echoes the embassy sent to Rome against Archelaus.

Herod Agrippa I A grandson of Herod the Great who briefly ruled all Judea and persecuted the church in Acts 12. What it was. Agrippa I grew up in Rome among the imperial family and was a friend of the future emperors Caligula and Claudius. Caligula gave him the former territories of Philip and of Antipas, and in AD 41 Claudius added Judea and Samaria, so that he ruled almost all his grandfather’s kingdom. He took care to please the Jewish people and was popular with them. In AD 44, at games in Caesarea, he was hailed as a god and died suddenly, a death described both in Acts and by Josephus, who says he was seized with violent pains and died five days later. In today’s terms. Agrippa was the last Jewish king to rule over Jerusalem. His reign over Judea lasted only about three years. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Acts calls him simply “Herod the king”. To win popularity he killed the apostle James, the brother of John, and arrested Peter, intending to execute him after Passover. But the church prayed, and the Lord sent his angel to free Peter. Soon after, Herod accepted worship as a god and was struck down because he did not give God the glory. Luke adds, “But the word of God increased and multiplied” (Acts 12:24). Persecutors die; the word of God goes on. Acts 12:1-3 About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword. And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. Agrippa I struck at the church’s leaders to please the crowds. Acts 12:23 Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. The king who took glory for himself was humbled by God.

Herod Agrippa II (with Bernice) The last of the Herodian kings, who heard Paul’s defence at Caesarea with his sister Bernice. What it was. Agrippa II was the son of Agrippa I. He was only seventeen when his father died in AD 44, so Judea went back to Roman governors. He later ruled territories to the north and east of Galilee, and Rome gave him oversight of the temple and the power to appoint high priests. He was well informed about Jewish customs and Scripture. Bernice was his sister; she lived with him for long periods, which caused scandalous rumours, and later became the companion of the Roman general Titus. Their sister Drusilla was the wife of the governor Felix. Agrippa sided with Rome in the Jewish revolt of AD 66 to 70, and died about AD 92 to 100. In today’s terms. Think of a client king in the empire’s service: Jewish in religion, Roman in loyalty, and asked by the new governor Festus for expert advice. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Acts 25 and 26, about AD 59, Agrippa and Bernice entered the audience hall “with great pomp”, and Paul, in chains, made his fullest defence. Paul appealed to the king’s knowledge of the prophets and pressed him to believe. Agrippa’s reply, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?”, shows a man near to the kingdom yet holding back. Jesus had foretold that his witnesses would stand before kings for his sake (Luke 21:12). Acts 25:13 Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. Agrippa and Bernice came to welcome the new governor. Acts 26:28 And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” Agrippa felt the force of Paul’s appeal but would not yield.

The Herod family at a glance A short guide to telling apart the different Herods in the New Testament. What it was. Several members of one family are called “Herod” in the New Testament, which easily confuses readers. Here they are in order. Herod the Great (king, 37 to 4 BC): the wise men and the killing of the infants (Matthew 2; Luke 1:5). His sons: Archelaus (ruler of Judea, 4 BC to AD 6), whom Joseph feared (Matthew 2:22); Herod Antipas (tetrarch of Galilee, 4 BC to AD 39), who beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus; and Philip the tetrarch (4 BC to AD 34), ruler of lands north-east of Galilee, who built Caesarea Philippi (Luke 3:1). His grandson: Herod Agrippa I (king, AD 41 to 44), who killed James and died at Caesarea (Acts 12). His great-grandchildren: Agrippa II, Bernice and Drusilla (Acts 24 to 26). In today’s terms. A simple rule: “Herod” in the birth stories is Herod the Great; “Herod” during Jesus’ ministry and trial is Antipas; “Herod” in Acts 12 is Agrippa I; and “Agrippa” in Acts 25 and 26 is Agrippa II. Herodias, Antipas’ wife, was also a granddaughter of Herod the Great. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The family spans the whole New Testament story, from Jesus’ birth to Paul’s imprisonment. One family of kings set itself against the true King again and again, and each passed away while his kingdom grew. Luke 3:1 In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, Luke names Antipas and Philip, two of Herod’s sons, alongside Tiberius and Pilate. Matthew 14:1 At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, Herod the tetrarch is Antipas, not his father.

Caesar Augustus The first Roman emperor, who ruled when Jesus was born. What it was. Born Octavian, he was the adopted heir of Julius Caesar. After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC he became sole ruler of the Roman world, and in 27 BC the Senate gave him the title “Augustus” (“revered one”). He ruled until his death in AD 14. He brought an end to decades of civil war and began the long “Roman peace” (Pax Romana), with good roads, safer seas and a common trading world. He was honoured in the east as a son of a god and a “saviour”, and the good news (gospel) of his birthday was celebrated in inscriptions. In today’s terms. He reigned for about 40 years. “Caesar” was his family name and became a title for the emperors who followed him, much as later rulers were called Kaiser or Tsar. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Luke tells us a decree of Augustus brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, so that the Christ was born in David’s town as Micah foretold (Micah 5:2). The mightiest man on earth unknowingly served God’s plan. And the peace, roads and common language of his empire became paths for the gospel. While Augustus was hailed as saviour and lord, the true Saviour, Christ the Lord, was born in a manger (Luke 2:11). God sent his Son “when the fullness of time had come”. Luke 2:1 In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. An emperor’s decree served God’s purpose to bring Jesus to Bethlehem. Galatians 4:4 But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, God chose the exact moment in history to send his Son.

Tiberius The Roman emperor during Jesus’ ministry, death and resurrection. What it was. Tiberius was the stepson and adopted heir of Augustus, and ruled from AD 14 to 37. He was an able general but a gloomy, suspicious man, and in his later years he withdrew to the island of Capri, leaving much of the government to others and holding treason trials in Rome. It was in his reign that Pontius Pilate governed Judea. The city of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee was named after him by Herod Antipas, and the “Sea of Tiberias” in John’s Gospel takes its name from that city. In today’s terms. Luke dates the start of John the Baptist’s ministry to “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar”, about AD 28 or 29 (scholars differ on how Luke counted the years). The silver denarius that circulated in Judea then usually bore Tiberius’ head and titles, calling him son of the divine Augustus. Why it matters when you read the Bible. When Jesus asked, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?”, the coin in his hand was almost certainly a denarius of Tiberius. Coins bearing Caesar’s image belong to Caesar; we who bear God’s image belong to God. At the trial, the cry “you are not Caesar’s friend” played on Pilate’s fear of the suspicious Tiberius (John 19:12). Luke 3:1 In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, Luke anchors the gospel story in world history. Mark 12:16-17 And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. The coin bore the emperor’s image; Jesus claims for God what bears God’s image.

Claudius The Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54, who expelled the Jews from Rome. What it was. Claudius became emperor unexpectedly after Caligula was murdered in AD 41. He was a scholarly man, mocked for a limp and a stammer, but a capable ruler. He gave Judea to his friend Herod Agrippa I. About AD 49 he ordered the Jews to leave Rome. The Roman historian Suetonius says this was because of disturbances “at the instigation of Chrestus”, which many scholars think is a garbled reference to arguments over Christ in Rome’s synagogues. His reign also saw a series of food shortages across the empire, including a severe famine in Judea in the mid to late 40s. In today’s terms. An inscription found at Delphi, dated to Claudius’ reign, mentions Gallio as governor of Achaia; it allows Paul’s stay in Corinth (Acts 18:12) to be dated to about AD 50 to 52, one of the firmest dates in the New Testament. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Claudius’ expulsion is why Paul met Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth: tentmakers like Paul, they became his co-workers and dear friends. Agabus’ prophecy of a famine “in the days of Claudius” moved the church at Antioch to send relief to Judea, an early example of Gentile and Jewish believers caring for one another (Acts 11:29-30). God uses emperors’ decrees and hard times to spread his church. Acts 18:2 And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, Claudius’ decree brought Aquila and Priscilla across Paul’s path. Acts 11:28 And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). The famine under Claudius prompted the church’s first relief offering.

Nero The Roman emperor from AD 54 to 68, to whom Paul appealed, and under whom Peter and Paul were probably martyred. What it was. Nero became emperor at sixteen. His early years, guided by his advisers, were reasonably good, but he grew increasingly cruel and self-indulgent: he had his own mother killed. In AD 64 a great fire destroyed much of Rome. The historian Tacitus says that, to stop rumours that he had started it, Nero blamed the Christians, and had many put to death horribly: torn by dogs, crucified, or burned as torches. He killed himself in AD 68 as the army turned against him. He is never named in the Bible. In today’s terms. When Paul says “I appeal to Caesar” (about AD 59), and when he greets the church from “Caesar’s household”, the Caesar is Nero. Early Christian tradition says that Peter was crucified and Paul beheaded in Rome under Nero, probably about AD 64 to 67. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Remember that Paul wrote Romans 13, calling Christians to honour the governing authorities as instituted by God, early in Nero’s reign. Peter wrote “Honour the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17) under the same ruler. Their obedience was not naive: they knew suffering might come, yet they trusted the King of kings. Even in Nero’s palace there were believers (Philippians 4:22), and the Lord stood by Paul at his trial (2 Timothy 4:17). Acts 25:11 I appeal to Caesar. Paul’s appeal to Caesar was an appeal to Nero. Philippians 4:22 All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household. The gospel had reached the emperor’s own household. Romans 13:1 Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Paul taught submission to authorities while Nero reigned.

Pontius Pilate The Roman governor of Judea who sentenced Jesus to be crucified. What it was. Pilate was the Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26 to 36. He lived mainly in Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at the feasts with troops to keep order. Josephus and Philo describe him as stubborn and harsh: he brought standards with Caesar’s image into Jerusalem, took temple money to build an aqueduct, and put down protests with force. Luke mentions Galileans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices. In AD 36 he was recalled to Rome after attacking a crowd of Samaritans. A stone inscribed with his name and title was found at Caesarea in 1961. In today’s terms. A prefect was a governor answerable to the emperor, with command of the local troops and the power of life and death. Pilate’s rule lasted about ten years. Why it matters when you read the Bible. All four Gospels show Pilate declaring Jesus innocent, yet handing him over to be crucified for fear of the crowd and of Caesar. He washed his hands, but could not wash away his guilt. Yet he played his part in God’s plan (Acts 4:27-28): the innocent one died in place of the guilty. Christians confess every Sunday that Jesus “suffered under Pontius Pilate”, which roots our faith in real history. John 18:38 Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him. Pilate declared Jesus not guilty. Matthew 27:24 So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves.” Pilate tried to disown a guilt he could not escape. 1 Timothy 6:13 I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, Jesus’ confession before Pilate is a pattern for every believer.

Felix The Roman governor of Judea who kept Paul in prison for two years at Caesarea. What it was. Antonius Felix governed Judea from about AD 52 to 59 or 60. He was a former slave, freed by the emperor’s family, and rose high through his brother Pallas, a powerful official in Rome. The historian Tacitus said he “exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave”. His rule was marked by brutal crackdowns on rebels, and Judea grew more unsettled under him. His wife Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I, whom he had persuaded to leave her first husband. In today’s terms. Felix was the governor before whom Paul was tried in Acts 24. He hoped for a bribe and so kept Paul waiting for two years, until he was recalled to Rome and replaced by Festus. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Felix heard the gospel personally, with Drusilla beside him. As Paul spoke of “righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment”, Felix was alarmed, and said “Go away for the present”. He often sent for Paul again, but there is no sign he ever believed. He is a sober warning against putting off repentance to a more convenient time: “now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Acts 24:24-25 After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” Felix trembled under the word, but delayed. Acts 24:27 When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. Self-interest kept Paul in prison two years.

Festus The Roman governor of Judea after Felix, who sent Paul to Rome. What it was. Porcius Festus succeeded Felix about AD 59 or 60 and governed Judea until his death in office about AD 62. Josephus portrays him as a fairer and more energetic governor than Felix or those who came after him, dealing firmly with bandits and rebels. Soon after his arrival the Jewish leaders asked him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, planning to ambush him on the way. When Festus asked Paul whether he would be tried in Jerusalem, Paul used his right as a Roman citizen and appealed to Caesar. In today’s terms. Think of a new governor inheriting a difficult file. Festus needed something to write to the emperor about Paul, so he asked King Agrippa II to hear him (Acts 25:26). Why it matters when you read the Bible. Festus summed up the case honestly but without understanding: it was a dispute “about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive”. That is the gospel in a sentence. When Paul spoke of the resurrection, Festus cried out that he was mad; Paul answered that he was speaking “true and rational words”. Festus’ decision fulfilled the Lord’s promise that Paul would testify in Rome (Acts 23:11). Acts 25:12 Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” Festus granted Paul’s appeal and sent him to Rome. Acts 25:19 Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. An outsider’s summary of the Christian message. Acts 26:24-25 And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. The resurrection sounded like madness to Festus, but Paul insisted it was true.

Quirinius The Roman governor of Syria named by Luke in connection with the census at Jesus’ birth. What it was. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was a senior Roman official and soldier. Josephus records that as governor of Syria in AD 6 he carried out a census in Judea, when Archelaus was removed. That census provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). Luke 2:2 links Jesus’ birth, before Herod’s death in 4 BC, with “the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria”. In today’s terms. This is a well-known puzzle and scholars differ on the answer. Some think Quirinius held an earlier command in the region before 4 BC; others translate Luke as “this registration was before Quirinius was governor”, distinguishing it from the famous census of AD 6; others suggest a registration begun under Herod was completed under Quirinius. Luke clearly knew of the later census, so he was not confused about it. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Luke wrote as a careful historian (Luke 1:1-4), and he has repeatedly been shown accurate in details of titles and places. Where we cannot yet fit every piece together, it is wise to hold our questions humbly rather than doubt the text. The point Luke makes is clear: God moved the machinery of the empire to bring Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, the city of David, at the right time. Luke 2:2 This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria. Luke ties the birth of Christ to a real Roman official and a real registration.

Kings of Israel and Judah The rulers of the two kingdoms into which Israel split after Solomon, from about 930 BC to 586 BC. What it was. After Solomon died (about 930 BC) the ten northern tribes rebelled against his son Rehoboam and made Jeroboam king (1 Kings 12). The north (Israel, capital Samaria) had 19 kings from several dynasties: Jeroboam I, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, Ahab, Ahaziah, Joram, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, Hoshea. Every one is judged to have done evil, following Jeroboam’s golden calves. The south (Judah, capital Jerusalem) had 19 kings and one queen, all of David’s line except the usurper Athaliah: Rehoboam, Abijam, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, Ahaziah, Athaliah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah. In today’s terms. Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC; Judah fell to Babylon in 586 BC. Kings, with Chronicles, tells the story; most of the prophets are dated by these reigns. Kings commended as doing right include Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, and above all Hezekiah and Josiah. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The long line of failing kings, even the best of them flawed, shows that Israel needed a better King. God had promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:16). After the exile no son of David reigned, until Jesus, the Son of David, came as the King the whole history was waiting for. 1 Kings 12:19-20 So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only. The kingdom divided, with only Judah staying loyal to David’s house. 2 Kings 18:5 He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him. Hezekiah’s trust in the Lord made him stand out among Judah’s kings. Isaiah 9:7 Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. The prophets looked beyond the failing kings to the Messiah’s endless reign.

Pharaoh The title of the kings of Egypt; several different pharaohs appear in Scripture. What it was. “Pharaoh” comes from Egyptian words meaning “great house”, the royal palace, and came to be used of the king himself, rather as we speak of “the Crown” or “the White House”. The Bible mentions many pharaohs. In Genesis, one took Sarah (Genesis 12) and another raised Joseph to power. In Exodus, a “new king who did not know Joseph” enslaved Israel, and a pharaoh, perhaps the same one or his successor, resisted Moses. Later pharaohs named in Scripture include Shishak, who plundered Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:25); Tirhakah (2 Kings 19:9); Neco, who killed Josiah at Megiddo; and Hophra (Jeremiah 44:30). Solomon married a pharaoh’s daughter. In today’s terms. The pharaohs of Genesis and Exodus are not named, and scholars differ on who they were. Taking 1 Kings 6:1 at face value dates the exodus to about 1446 BC, and some identify the pharaoh of that time as Amenhotep II; others prefer a later date. Shishak is usually identified with Shoshenq I (about 925 BC). Why it matters when you read the Bible. Pharaoh of the exodus is the great picture of a proud ruler who sets himself against God. Paul uses him to show God’s sovereignty: God raised him up to display his power and make his name known in all the earth. Out of Egypt God redeemed his people, and Matthew shows Jesus, the true Israel, also called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15). Exodus 1:8 Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. A new pharaoh turned from favour to oppression. Romans 9:17 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” God used Pharaoh’s hardness to proclaim his name in all the earth. 2 Kings 23:29 In his days Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt went up to the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates. King Josiah went to meet him, and Pharaoh Neco killed him at Megiddo, as soon as he saw him. Pharaoh Neco is one of the named pharaohs of Scripture.

Nebuchadnezzar The king of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and carried Judah into exile. What it was. Nebuchadnezzar II reigned over Babylon from 605 to 562 BC, the greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian empire. In 605 BC he defeated Egypt at Carchemish and took the first captives from Jerusalem, including Daniel and his friends. In 597 BC he took King Jehoiachin, Ezekiel and thousands more to Babylon. When Zedekiah rebelled, his army besieged Jerusalem and in 586 BC burned the temple, the palace and the city. He also rebuilt Babylon on a vast scale, with its famous Ishtar Gate. In today’s terms. He reigned about 43 years. Bricks stamped with his name have been found by the thousands in Babylon’s ruins, and the Babylonian Chronicles record his capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God’s “servant”: not a believer, but the instrument by which the Lord judged his people’s sin, as he had warned. In Daniel, this proud king learns that “the Most High rules the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:25). After being humbled, he praises the King of heaven. Daniel 2 shows God’s kingdom, the stone cut without hands, outlasting all the kingdoms of men; it is the kingdom Christ brings. Jeremiah 25:9 and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, God called Nebuchadnezzar his servant in bringing judgment. 2 Kings 25:9 And he burned the house of the LORD and the king’s house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down. Nebuchadnezzar’s army destroyed Solomon’s temple in 586 BC. Daniel 4:37 Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble. The proud king was humbled and praised the King of heaven.

Cyrus The Persian king who conquered Babylon and allowed the Jews to return home and rebuild the temple. What it was. Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire. In 539 BC his forces took Babylon, apparently with little fighting, the same night Belshazzar feasted (Daniel 5). In his first year as ruler of Babylon, about 538 BC, he issued a decree allowing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem, rebuild the temple and take back the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried away (Ezra 1). His policy of letting deported peoples return home and restore their shrines is also recorded on the Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription now in the British Museum. He died about 530 BC. In today’s terms. His decree came about seventy years after the first exiles were taken in 605 BC, as Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 29:10). His empire went on to stretch from the Aegean Sea to India, the largest the world had then seen. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Isaiah named Cyrus long before his birth, calling him the Lord’s “shepherd” and even his “anointed”, raised up to rebuild Jerusalem. A pagan king became a picture of a greater deliverer: just as Cyrus set the captives free to return home, Christ, the true Anointed One, sets his people free from the captivity of sin and brings them home to God. Isaiah 44:28 who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose’; saying of Jerusalem, ‘She shall be built,’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation shall be laid.’” Isaiah named Cyrus as God’s shepherd long before he appeared. Isaiah 45:1 Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed: The Lord called Cyrus his anointed, an instrument of his purpose. Ezra 1:1-2 In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, Cyrus’ decree fulfilled the word of the Lord by Jeremiah.

Threshing Floor and Winnowing The threshing floor was the flat, open place where harvested grain was beaten loose from its stalks and then tossed in the wind to separate it from the chaff. What it was. After the harvest, sheaves of wheat or barley were carried to a hard, flat patch of rock or beaten earth, usually on higher ground where the wind blew. Oxen walked round and round over the stalks, or dragged a heavy wooden sledge studded with stones, to break the grain out of the husks (threshing). Then the farmer used a wooden fork or shovel to toss the mixture into the air, often in the evening breeze. The heavy grain fell back to the floor, while the light chaff, the dry husks, blew away (winnowing). Farmers often slept beside the pile to guard it. In today’s terms. Think of it as a combine harvester done by hand, by animals and by the wind, and taking days rather than minutes. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This scene lies behind Ruth meeting Boaz at night, and David buying Araunah’s threshing floor, the site where the temple was later built. Above all it gives the Bible a picture of judgment. The wicked are “like chaff that the wind drives away”. John the Baptist warned that Christ comes with his winnowing fork in his hand. The same Lord who separates also gathers: his wheat is brought safely into his barn. Ruth 3:2 See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. Winnowing was done in the evening breeze, and the owner stayed by his grain. Psalm 1:4 The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away. Chaff is light and worthless: a picture of a life with no root in God. Matthew 3:12 His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. Christ is the one who will finally separate his people from the ungodly. The question every reader faces is whether they are wheat gathered in by Christ or chaff blown away.

Winepress A winepress was a pair of basins, usually cut into rock, where grapes were trampled underfoot and the juice ran off to be made into wine. What it was. At the grape harvest in late summer, grapes were piled into an upper vat, often hollowed out of the bedrock in or near the vineyard. Workers trod them with bare feet, holding on to ropes or one another, and often singing. The juice ran down a channel into a lower vat, where it was collected and put into jars or skins to ferment. The treaders’ legs and clothes were soon splashed and stained deep red. In today’s terms. Picture a stone paddling pool full of grapes, with people stamping in it until they looked as if they were spattered with blood. Why it matters when you read the Bible. That red stain explains why the winepress became a picture of God’s wrath. In Isaiah the Lord comes from battle with stained garments, having “trodden the winepress alone”. Revelation shows Christ, the returning King, treading “the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God”. The gospel shows the other side: before he comes as judge, Christ bore that wrath himself on the cross for all who trust in him. Isaiah 63:3 I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me The Lord alone acts to judge his enemies and save his people. Revelation 14:19 So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. The final judgment is pictured as a harvest crushed in a winepress. Revelation 19:15 He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. Christ himself carries out God’s judgment when he returns.

Millstone A millstone was one of a pair of heavy stones used to grind grain into flour. What it was. Every household needed flour every day, so grinding was one of the first jobs of the morning, usually done by women or servants. The simplest mill was a flat lower stone with a smaller upper stone rubbed back and forth across it. Later, round hand mills (querns) were used: the upper stone was turned on the lower one by a wooden handle, often by two women sitting facing each other. Larger mills, with an upper stone as big as a table-top, were turned by a donkey walking in a circle. In today’s terms. A hand millstone weighed perhaps as much as a heavy suitcase. The donkey-driven kind Jesus mentions could weigh several hundred pounds (well over 100 kg), far beyond what a man could lift. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because the mill was needed to feed the family, the law forbade taking one as security for a loan: that would be “taking a life in pledge”. The sound of grinding meant ordinary life going on, and its silence meant ruin. Jesus’ warning is chilling: it would be better to be drowned with a donkey’s millstone round your neck than to lead one of his little ones into sin. Christ cares fiercely for the weakest believers. Deuteronomy 24:6 No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge. The mill was so necessary for daily bread that God protected it in law. Matthew 24:41 Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left. Grinding was ordinary daily work, which is where Christ’s return will find people. Matthew 18:6 it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea. The heaviest stone imaginable shows how seriously Christ takes harm done to his little ones.

Wineskins Wineskins were bags made from the whole skin of a goat, used to hold and carry wine, water or milk. What it was. A goat was skinned in one piece, the openings at the legs and neck were tied or sewn shut, and the hide was treated so that it would hold liquid. New wine was poured into fresh skins while it was still fermenting. A new skin was soft and could stretch as the wine gave off gas. An old skin had already been stretched once and had become dry and brittle, so if it was filled with new wine it would split. In today’s terms. A wineskin held a few gallons (perhaps 10 to 20 litres), and an old one was like a worn rubber balloon: blow it up again and it bursts. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus used this everyday fact to show that his coming was something new. The joy of the kingdom could not simply be poured into the old forms of religious ritual, such as the Pharisees’ rules of fasting, without bursting them. The gospel is not a patch on the old system but the fulfilment of everything it pointed to. Elsewhere worn-out skins are a sign of a long journey, as the Gibeonites pretended when they tricked Joshua. Matthew 9:17 Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved. The new life Christ brings needs a new kind of vessel. Joshua 9:13 These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. Burst skins were meant to suggest a long journey: a reminder to seek the Lord’s counsel before acting.

Oil Lamp The ordinary lamp of Bible times was a small clay dish holding olive oil, with a wick of flax burning at its spout. What it was. A lamp was a palm-sized bowl of baked clay, often with a pinched or covered spout for the wick and a hole on top for pouring in oil. It gave a small, steady flame, and was set on a stand or in a niche in the wall so its light would spread through the room. Most homes were single rooms with small windows, so a lamp was kept burning through the night. A lamp held only a little oil and had to be refilled, and wise people kept a jug of oil to hand. In today’s terms. One lamp gave about as much light as a single candle and burned for a few hours on a filling. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Knowing how small the light was makes the Bible’s pictures vivid. God’s word is “a lamp to my feet”: enough light for the next step, on a dark path. Jesus said no one hides a lamp under a basket, so his disciples must let their light be seen. In the parable of the ten virgins, the foolish had no oil left when the bridegroom came, a warning to be ready for Christ’s return. Psalm 119:105 Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. Scripture gives light for each step of the believer’s way. Matthew 5:15 Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. A lamp exists to give light; so do the lives of Christ’s people. Matthew 25:8 Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out. Lamps needed refilling; readiness for Christ cannot be borrowed at the last minute.

Houses and Flat Roofs Most houses in Bible lands were simple buildings of stone or mud brick with a flat roof that was used as an extra room. What it was. An ordinary house had thick walls of stone or sun-dried brick and few, small windows. Many families lived in one or two rooms, sometimes with the animals sheltered in part of the ground floor at night. The roof was made of wooden beams covered with branches and a thick layer of packed clay, rolled flat after the rains. Steps outside led up to it. People dried flax and fruit on the roof, slept there on hot nights, and went up to pray. The law required a low wall (a parapet) around it so no one fell off. In today’s terms. Think of a roof terrace or a flat-roofed balcony that was part of daily living, not just a covering. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This explains several scenes. Rahab hid the spies under stalks of flax on her roof. Peter went up on the housetop at noon to pray. The friends of the paralysed man could climb up, dig through the clay and branches, and lower him to Jesus. The parapet law shows God’s care for neighbours’ lives even in building rules: love takes thought for others’ safety. Deuteronomy 22:8 When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it. Because people used the roof, love for neighbour required a safety wall. Mark 2:4 they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. A roof of beams, branches and clay could be opened by determined friends. Acts 10:9 Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. The flat roof was a quiet place for prayer.

Wells and Cisterns Wells were shafts dug down to underground water, and cisterns were pits cut in rock to store rainwater for the dry season. What it was. Rain falls in the land of Israel only in winter, so water had to be found or saved. A well reached down to a spring or to groundwater, and a good well was a treasure worth fighting over, as Abraham and Isaac found. A cistern was a bottle-shaped pit cut into the rock and lined with plaster to catch rain running off roofs and hillsides. If the plaster cracked, the water leaked away. An empty cistern made a ready prison: Joseph and Jeremiah were both thrown into one. In today’s terms. Jacob’s well near Sychar is still more than 100 feet (30 m) deep. A cistern was like a stone water tank, holding rain to last through a summer with no rain at all. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jeremiah’s picture is sharp: God’s people turned from “the fountain of living waters”, a fresh spring, to dig cracked cisterns of their own. At Jacob’s well Jesus offered the Samaritan woman “living water”, the life of the Spirit that never runs dry. He is the spring our hearts look for in every leaking substitute. Jeremiah 2:13 they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water. Turning from God to idols is like leaving a spring for a leaking tank. John 4:11 Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? The woman thought of a deep well; Jesus meant the life he alone gives. Genesis 37:24 And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it. A dry cistern could serve as a prison, as it did for Joseph.

Sandals and Washing Feet People wore simple leather sandals on dusty roads, so washing a guest’s feet was a common act of welcome, usually done by the lowest servant. What it was. A sandal was a sole of leather or wood tied to the foot with leather straps. Roads and village paths were dusty in summer and muddy in winter, and people walked almost everywhere. On arriving at a house, a guest would remove his sandals, and the host would offer water to wash his feet, or have a servant do it. Untying and carrying a master’s sandals and washing his feet were jobs for a slave; even a disciple was not expected to do them for his teacher. In today’s terms. It was like a host taking your wet coat and muddy boots at the door, except that the host’s servant knelt and washed the dirt off you. Why it matters when you read the Bible. John the Baptist said he was not worthy even to untie Christ’s sandal strap. Jesus rebuked Simon the Pharisee for giving him no water for his feet. Then, on the night before he died, the Lord himself took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet. He was showing the humble love that would go to the cross to wash sinners clean, and calling his people to serve one another in the same way. Mark 1:7 After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. Untying sandals was a slave’s task, yet John felt unworthy even of that. Luke 7:44 I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. Failing to offer water for the feet was a failure of basic courtesy. John 13:5 Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. The Lord took the lowest servant’s place, a picture of his saving humility.

Clothing (Tunic and Cloak) Ordinary clothing was a tunic worn next to the skin and a heavier cloak worn over it, which also served as a blanket at night. What it was. The tunic was a long shirt of linen or wool reaching to the knees or ankles, held in at the waist by a belt or sash. For work or running, a man tucked its hem into his belt, which is what “gird up your loins” means. Over it went the cloak, a large square of woollen cloth wrapped around the body. A poor man might own only one cloak, and he slept in it. Women’s clothing was similar but longer and distinct from men’s. In today’s terms. The tunic was like a long shirt or nightshirt, and the cloak was coat and blanket in one. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because a poor man needed his cloak to sleep, the law said one taken as a pledge must be returned by sunset. Jesus’ words about giving your cloak as well as your tunic meant giving up even what the law protected for you. At the cross the soldiers gambled for his seamless tunic, fulfilling Psalm 22, and he was left with nothing. He was stripped so that we could be clothed with his righteousness. Exodus 22:26 If ever you take your neighbor’s cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, A cloak was a poor man’s bedding, so God protected it. Matthew 5:40 And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. Christ calls his people to a generosity beyond their legal rights. John 19:23 also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, Even Jesus’ last garment was taken from him at the cross.

Meals and Reclining at Table At formal meals and feasts in New Testament times, guests did not sit on chairs but reclined on couches or cushions around a low table. What it was. Everyday meals were simple and eaten sitting on the floor or on mats. But at a banquet, following Greek and Roman custom, guests lay on their left side, propped on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out away from the table, and ate with the right hand. Often three couches were set in a U shape round the table, and seats nearer the host were places of honour. To share a meal was to share friendship; Jews would not normally eat with people they thought unclean. In today’s terms. Picture people lying on sofas round a coffee table, heads towards the food and feet pointing outwards. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This makes sense of the woman who came up behind Jesus and wept over his feet: his feet were stretched out behind him. It explains how John, reclining next to Jesus, could lean back against his chest to ask a question. It also shows why eating with tax collectors and sinners caused offence. Christ welcomed sinners to his table, and he still promises to come in and eat with anyone who opens the door to him. Luke 7:38 and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears Reclining guests had their feet behind them, within reach of someone standing there. John 13:23 One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side, At the Last Supper the disciples reclined, so John lay close beside Jesus. Revelation 3:20 If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me. Sharing a meal is Christ’s picture of close fellowship with his people.

Bread Bread was the main food of ordinary people in Bible times, so central that “bread” could simply mean food. What it was. Bread was baked every day, usually by the women of the house, from flour ground that morning. Wheat bread was best; poorer people ate barley bread. Loaves were flat and round, baked on hot stones, on the inside wall of a clay oven, or on a metal plate over a fire. Bread was not cut with a knife but torn or broken by hand, so “breaking bread” came to mean sharing a meal. Bread was also offered to God in the tabernacle as the bread of the Presence. In today’s terms. A loaf was more like a pitta or a flatbread than a sliced sandwich loaf, and it made up perhaps half or more of what people ate each day. Why it matters when you read the Bible. When we pray “Give us this day our daily bread”, we ask for everything we need to live. God fed Israel with manna, bread from heaven, in the wilderness. Jesus was born in Bethlehem, whose name means “house of bread”, and he said, “I am the bread of life.” He broke bread with his disciples, and in the Lord’s Supper the broken bread shows his body given for us. Matthew 6:11 Give us this day our daily bread, Bread stands for all the daily needs we receive from our Father. John 6:35 I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger Christ is the true food that satisfies the soul. Luke 24:30 he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. Bread was broken by hand, and the risen Lord was known in the breaking of it.

Weddings and Betrothal A Jewish marriage began with a binding betrothal and was completed, often about a year later, when the bridegroom brought his bride home for the wedding feast. What it was. Betrothal was much more than a modern engagement. A contract was agreed between families, and a bride price was usually paid. From then on the couple were legally husband and wife and could be separated only by divorce, though they did not yet live together. On the wedding day the bridegroom and his friends went, often in the evening, to fetch the bride from her father’s house. A torch-lit procession brought her to his home, and the feast could last up to a week. In today’s terms. Betrothal was like being legally married but living apart until the wedding, which is why Joseph planned a quiet divorce. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This explains Mary and Joseph’s situation, and the parable of the ten virgins waiting for the bridegroom to arrive at night. Scripture calls the church Christ’s bride. Believers are now betrothed to him, bound to him and loved by him, waiting for him to come and take us home. History ends with a wedding: “the marriage of the Lamb has come.” Matthew 1:18 When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Betrothal was binding, though the couple did not yet live together. Matthew 25:10 the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. The bridegroom’s arrival began the feast; the unready were left outside. Revelation 19:7 for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; The story of redemption ends with the marriage of Christ and his church.

Burial Customs and Tombs In Bible lands the dead were usually buried on the day they died, wrapped in cloth with spices and laid in a family tomb, often cut into rock. What it was. In a hot climate burial could not wait, so it normally took place within a day. The body was washed, anointed with oils and spices, and wrapped in strips of linen, with a separate cloth for the face. Poorer people were buried in simple graves in the ground. Families who could afford it used a cave or a tomb cut into the rock, with ledges inside for the bodies. The entrance was closed by a large stone, sometimes round and rolled in a groove. After a year or so the bones might be gathered into a stone box (an ossuary) to make room. In today’s terms. A rock tomb was like a small room carved into a hillside, closed with a stone too heavy for one person to move. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This background fills in the Gospels. Lazarus lay four days in a cave tomb with a stone across it. Jesus’ body was wrapped with about seventy-five pounds of spices and laid in a new tomb belonging to Joseph of Arimathea, as Isaiah foretold.
