The great stone, the guard, and the folded grave cloths all testify that the tomb was really empty on the third day, because Christ had risen. John 19:40 So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews. Jesus was buried according to normal Jewish custom. John 11:38 Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Many family tombs were caves sealed with a stone. Matthew 27:60 and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away. The new rock tomb and great stone make the empty tomb all the more striking.

Mourning Customs (Sackcloth and Ashes) In Bible times people showed grief and repentance outwardly, by tearing their clothes, wearing sackcloth and putting ashes or dust on their heads. What it was. Sackcloth was a rough, dark cloth woven from goat or camel hair, the material used for grain sacks. Mourners wore it next to the skin instead of their normal clothes. They tore the front of their garments, sat in ashes or threw dust on their heads, fasted, and wept aloud. Funerals included wailing and flute players, sometimes hired professionals. Mourning for a close relative usually lasted seven days, and for great leaders thirty days. The same signs were used for national disaster and for repentance before God. In today’s terms. It was like wearing rough sacking in public and sitting in the ashes of the fire: a deliberate way of saying, “I am broken.” Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jacob put on sackcloth for Joseph; the king of Nineveh left his throne and sat in ashes when Jonah preached. Jesus said that Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes had they seen his miracles. God wants the heart behind the sign (“rend your hearts and not your garments,” says Joel). And he promises that in Christ he will give his people “a beautiful headdress instead of ashes”. Genesis 37:34 Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days. Tearing garments and wearing sackcloth were signs of deep grief. Jonah 3:6 he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. A king exchanged royal robes for sackcloth as a sign of repentance. Matthew 11:21 they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Jesus used the familiar signs to speak of true repentance.

Slavery in the Ancient World Slavery, in which one person was owned by or bound to serve another, was a normal part of life throughout the ancient world, though it differed in important ways from later race-based slavery. What it was. People became slaves through war, debt, being born to slaves, or being sold by poor families. In Israel, God’s law limited it sharply. A fellow Israelite who sold himself because of debt was to be set free after six years and sent away with provisions. Kidnapping a person to sell was punished by death. Runaway slaves were not to be handed back. In the Roman Empire slaves were very many, perhaps a sixth to a third of people in some cities, though scholars differ. Some were labourers and some were managers, teachers or doctors. In today’s terms. Many slaves in Israel were closer to bonded labourers working off a debt. Roman slavery, though, could be harsh, and a slave had few rights. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The New Testament often calls believers “slaves” (servants) of Christ, and speaks of redemption, the price paid to free a slave. Paul sent the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon as “a beloved brother”, a word that undermined the whole system from within. Most of all, the Son of God took the form of a servant and gave his life as a ransom to set sinners free. Exodus 21:2 When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing. Israel’s law put a limit on servitude among God’s people. Philemon 16 no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother In Christ master and slave become brothers. Mark 10:45 For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. A ransom was the price paid to free a captive or slave.

Shepherds and Sheepfolds Shepherds looked after flocks of sheep and goats, leading them to pasture by day and keeping them safe in a walled sheepfold at night. What it was. A shepherd lived outdoors with his flock for much of the year. He led them from the front, called them by name, found grass and water, carried weak lambs, and fought off wolves, lions and bears with his staff and club. At night the sheep were brought into a fold, a ring of rough stone walls, sometimes topped with thorns, with one narrow opening. The shepherd might lie across the gap himself, becoming the door. By Jesus’ day shepherds were often looked down on as rough and unreliable. In today’s terms. A shepherd was security guard, guide and nurse to his flock all at once, often working through the night. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Kings and leaders were called shepherds, and David was taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel. Psalm 23 says “The LORD is my shepherd.” The good news of Christ’s birth came first to humble shepherds in the fields. Jesus called himself the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Pastors are under-shepherds, serving the chief Shepherd. Psalm 23:1 The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. God himself provides for and protects his people like a shepherd. Luke 2:8 And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. Shepherds stayed with their flocks at night, and they were the first to hear of Christ’s birth. John 10:11 I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Jesus gave his life to save his flock.

Fishing on the Sea of Galilee Fishing was a major trade around the Sea of Galilee, the freshwater lake where several of Jesus’ disciples worked as fishermen. What it was. The Sea of Galilee is a lake fed by the Jordan, lying about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level, with hills around it. Winds can rush down the hills and whip up sudden storms. Fishermen worked from wooden boats with oars and a small sail, often at night. They used a cast net thrown by hand from the shore, and larger dragnets let down between boats and drawn together. Nets had to be washed and mended after every trip. Fishing families like those of Peter and Andrew, and James and John, ran small businesses, sometimes with hired men. In today’s terms. The lake is about 13 miles long and 8 miles wide (21 by 13 km). A first-century boat found in its mud in 1986 is about 27 feet (8 m) long, big enough for a crew of a dozen or so. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This explains why the fishermen knew a catch in daylight was unlikely, and why their nets breaking showed Jesus’ power. Jesus called them to become “fishers of men”, gathering people into God’s kingdom. After his resurrection he met them again by the lake and filled their nets, showing that their work for him would bear fruit by his word. Mark 1:16-17 he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” Jesus called ordinary working fishermen to a new kind of fishing. Luke 5:6 And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. The huge catch, after a fruitless night, showed Christ’s lordship over creation. John 21:6 So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish. The risen Lord again directed their work and blessed it.

Roads and Travel Most people in Bible times travelled on foot along rough tracks, though by New Testament times the Romans had built paved roads across their empire. What it was. Ordinary travellers walked, perhaps with a donkey to carry baggage; the wealthy rode donkeys, mules or, later, horses and carriages. Most roads were dirt tracks, dusty or muddy by season. The Romans built well-engineered stone roads for their armies, which also carried merchants and missionaries like Paul. Travel was dangerous: robbers hid in lonely places, so people went in groups, as families did on pilgrimage to Jerusalem for the feasts. In today’s terms. A day’s journey on foot was about 20 miles (30 km). The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho runs about 17 miles (27 km) and drops more than 3,000 feet (900 m) through barren hills, perfect country for robbers. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This brings Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan to life. It explains why Jesus could walk unrecognised beside two disciples on the seven-mile road to Emmaus, and why Paul’s journeys took so long. Isaiah pictures workmen levelling a highway for a coming king; John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ, the King who himself is “the way”. Isaiah 40:3 In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Roads were prepared for a king’s arrival; John prepared for Christ. Luke 10:30 A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers The lonely road down to Jericho was well known for robbers. Luke 24:13 That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, Walking such distances was ordinary, and the risen Christ joined them on the way.

Letters and Scrolls Books in Bible times were written by hand on long rolls of papyrus or leather called scrolls, and letters were usually dictated to a scribe and carried by hand. What it was. Papyrus was a paper made from reeds; parchment was fine, treated animal skin. Sheets were joined into a long strip and rolled round a stick, and readers unrolled it with one hand while rolling it up with the other. Books bound with pages (a codex) came into common use only around the time of the apostles, and Christians took to them early. Letters followed a set pattern: sender, recipient, greeting, then the message. Writers often dictated to a trained scribe and added a greeting in their own hand. There was no public post for ordinary people, so letters went with trusted friends. In today’s terms. A long scroll was cumbersome: the Great Isaiah Scroll found near the Dead Sea is about 24 feet (7.3 m) long. Finding a passage took real effort. Why it matters when you read the Bible. This lies behind Jesus being handed the scroll of Isaiah in Nazareth and unrolling it to find his place. Tertius, Paul’s scribe, sends his own greeting in Romans. Paul, near death, asked Timothy to bring “the parchments”. God chose these humble means to give and preserve his inspired word for us. Luke 4:17 And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, Synagogue Scripture was read from scrolls, and Jesus found the passage about himself. Romans 16:22 I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord. Paul dictated his letters to a scribe, who here adds his own greeting. 2 Timothy 4:13 also the books, and above all the parchments. Even in prison Paul valued his books and writings.

Hospitality Hospitality, welcoming strangers and travellers into one’s home with food, shelter and protection, was a sacred duty in the Bible’s world. What it was. There were few inns, and those were often rough places. So travellers depended on the kindness of local people. A host would offer water to wash the guest’s feet, a meal, a place to sleep and protection while the guest was under his roof. To refuse hospitality was shameful. Abraham ran to meet three strangers and prepared a feast for them. In the early church, Christians travelling to preach relied on believers opening their homes, and elders were to be hospitable. In today’s terms. It was as though every household was expected to act as a free guesthouse for whoever turned up at the door. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Abraham and Lot entertained angels without at first knowing it, which Hebrews recalls. Israel was to love the stranger, remembering they had been strangers in Egypt. Hospitality reflects the gospel itself: God welcomed us when we were strangers and enemies, and Christ prepares a place for us at his table. So Christians are to open their homes “without grumbling”. Genesis 18:4 Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, Abraham’s welcome shows the warm customs of hospitality. Hebrews 13:2 Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Hospitality remains a Christian duty, and it may bring unexpected blessing. 1 Peter 4:9 Show hospitality to one another without grumbling. Welcoming others is to be done gladly.

Inheritance and the Firstborn In Israel the firstborn son received a double share of his father’s inheritance and became head of the family, a privilege called the birthright. What it was. When a father died, his property was divided among his sons, but the eldest received twice what each of the others did, and with it the duty to lead the family and care for its members. If there were no sons, daughters could inherit, as with the daughters of Zelophehad. The land itself was God’s gift and was meant to stay within the family and tribe. Every firstborn son and animal belonged to the Lord in a special way, because God spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover; sons were redeemed (bought back) by a payment. In today’s terms. With three sons, the estate was split four ways, and the eldest got two of the four parts, half of everything. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Esau despised his birthright and sold it for a bowl of stew. Again and again God passed over the elder for the younger, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim, David, showing that his blessing is by grace, not by right of birth. Christ is called the firstborn: not the first created, but the one with the highest rank, the heir of all things. In him believers become “fellow heirs”. Deuteronomy 21:17 by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his. The firstborn’s double share was protected by law. Genesis 25:33 So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Esau treated a great privilege as worthless. Colossians 1:18 He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent. Firstborn here means first in rank and in resurrection.

Gate of the City The gate of a walled city was its main public meeting place, where elders sat to judge cases, witness agreements and conduct business. What it was. A city gate was a strong building, not just a door. Many had a passage with several chambers on each side, with benches where people could sit, and an open square just inside or outside. Since everyone passed through it, the gate was the town’s court, council chamber, market and noticeboard. The elders, the senior men of the town, sat there to settle disputes and confirm sales and marriages. To sit “in the gate” was to hold a place of respect and responsibility. In today’s terms. The gate was the town hall, law court and market square combined, all in the busiest spot in town. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Boaz went to the gate to settle the matter of Ruth before the elders. The husband of the excellent wife in Proverbs is respected “in the gates”. The prophets demanded justice “in the gate”, where the poor were often cheated. Hebrews notes that Jesus suffered outside the city gate, cast out in shame, so that we might be made holy. Ruth 4:1 Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. The gate was where legal matters were settled before witnesses. Proverbs 31:23 Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. Sitting in the gate was a mark of honour and responsibility. Amos 5:15 Hate evil, and love good, and establish justice in the gate The gate was the court, where God demanded fair dealing.

Hyssop Hyssop was a small, bushy, sweet-smelling plant whose branches were used like a brush to sprinkle blood or water in cleansing rites. What it was. The hyssop of the Bible was probably not the garden herb of that name today, but a kind of wild marjoram (Syrian oregano) that grows in cracks in walls and rocks. It has many small, hairy leaves that hold liquid well. A bunch tied together made a handy sprinkler. Hyssop was used at the first Passover to daub lamb’s blood on the doorposts, and in the law to sprinkle blood or water for cleansing people healed of skin disease and those made unclean by touching the dead. In today’s terms. Picture a small bunch of thyme or oregano tied together and dipped in liquid to sprinkle it. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because of these rites, hyssop came to stand for cleansing from sin. David prayed, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean.” At the cross a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on a hyssop branch, a quiet reminder that he is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood cleanses all who trust him. Exodus 12:22 Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood Hyssop applied the Passover blood that saved Israel’s firstborn. Psalm 51:7 Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. David asks God himself to do the cleansing that the rites pictured. John 19:29 so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. Hyssop appears at the death of Christ, the Passover Lamb.

Mustard Seed The mustard seed, a tiny seed that grows into a large shrub, was Jesus’ picture of how the kingdom of God starts small and grows great. What it was. The plant was probably black mustard, grown for its seeds, which were used for flavouring and medicine. A seed is only about 1 mm across, and it was the smallest seed that farmers in Galilee normally sowed; “small as a mustard seed” was a common saying. Yet in a single season it can grow into a bush 8 to 10 feet (about 3 m) tall, sturdy enough for birds to perch in its branches. In today’s terms. A mustard seed is about the size of the full stop at the end of this sentence. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Jesus’ kingdom began with a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve disciples and a cross, which looked like nothing. Yet it has grown to fill the world, and people from every nation find shelter in it. Jesus also said faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains, because what matters is not the size of our faith but the greatness of the God it trusts. Matthew 13:31 The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. The kingdom begins small and hidden. Matthew 13:32 It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree From a tiny start comes great growth. Matthew 17:20 if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move Even small faith is mighty because it rests on a mighty God.

Fig Tree The fig tree was one of the most common fruit trees in Israel, prized for its sweet fruit and its broad, shady leaves. What it was. Fig trees grow to about 15 to 20 feet (5 or 6 m), with large leaves that give deep shade. They usually bear fruit twice a year. In spring, small green early figs appear along with, or even before, the leaves; the main crop ripens in late summer. Figs were eaten fresh, dried, or pressed into cakes. Because the early fruit comes with the leaves, a tree covered in leaves but with no fruit at all was a sign it would bear nothing that year. In today’s terms. A fig in leaf with no fruit was like a shop with its lights on but empty shelves. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves to cover their shame. “Every man under his vine and under his fig tree” was the Bible’s picture of peace and plenty. The fig tree often stands for Israel. When Jesus cursed a leafy fig tree with no fruit, he was acting out God’s judgment on a nation, and a temple, full of religious show but bearing no fruit for God. He looks for real fruit in his people. Genesis 3:7 And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths. The large fig leaves were the first human attempt to cover sin. Micah 4:4 but they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid Sitting under your own fig tree is a picture of God’s peace. Mark 11:13 When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. Leaves promised fruit, but there was none: a picture of empty religion.

Olive Tree and Olive Oil The olive tree was one of the most valuable trees in Israel, and its oil was used for food, light, medicine and anointing. What it was. Olive trees grow slowly and can live for hundreds of years, sending up new shoots even from an old stump. In autumn the olives were beaten from the branches with poles. They were then crushed in a press, and the oil was squeezed out. Olive oil was used for cooking, for lamps, for soothing wounds, as a soap and skin oil, and in worship. Priests and kings were anointed by having oil poured on their heads. In today’s terms. Olive oil was the cooking oil, lamp fuel, medicine and skin cream of the ancient world all in one bottle. Why it matters when you read the Bible. The Hebrew word “Messiah” and the Greek word “Christ” both mean “Anointed One”: Jesus is the one anointed by God as Prophet, Priest and King. Gethsemane, where he prayed in agony, means “oil press”. David pictured himself as a green olive tree in God’s house. Paul compares God’s people to an olive tree, into which Gentile believers have been grafted like wild branches. Psalm 52:8 But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever. The long-lived, fruitful olive pictures the believer who trusts God. Psalm 23:5 you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Oil on the head was a sign of honour and blessing for a guest. Romans 11:17 and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, Gentile believers are grafted into God’s one people.

Vine and Vineyard The grapevine was one of the main crops of Israel, and the vineyard became one of the Bible’s favourite pictures of God’s people. What it was. A vineyard was planted on a sunny hillside cleared of stones. The owner built a wall or hedge to keep out animals, a watchtower for a guard at harvest, and a winepress cut in the rock. Vines needed years of care before they bore well: digging, pruning dead and unfruitful wood, and propping up branches. Grapes were picked in late summer and eaten fresh, dried as raisins, or made into wine. In today’s terms. A vineyard was a long-term investment, like planting an orchard you will tend for decades. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Israel is the vine God brought out of Egypt and the vineyard he planted, yet it gave him only sour grapes. Jesus told parables about vineyards and their tenants. Then he said, “I am the vine; you are the branches.” Christ is the true Israel, the vine that bears the fruit God looked for, and his people bear fruit only by being joined to him. Psalm 80:8 You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. Israel is pictured as a vine God transplanted into the land. Isaiah 5:7 For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel God tended his people and looked for the fruit of justice. John 15:5 I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit Fruitfulness comes only from union with Christ.

Wheat and Tares (Weeds) Wheat was the most important grain of Israel, and the “tares” or weeds of Jesus’ parable were probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks just like wheat as it grows. What it was. Wheat was sown in late autumn after the first rains and harvested in late spring and early summer. Darnel grows among wheat and looks almost identical until the ears form. Its grains are often infected with a fungus that makes them toxic, causing dizziness and sickness if ground into flour. Pulling it up early would damage the wheat, since the roots tangle together, so farmers waited and sorted it out at harvest. Sowing weeds in an enemy’s field was a known act of spite. In today’s terms. Think of a weed that looks exactly like your lawn until it goes to seed. Why it matters when you read the Bible. In Jesus’ parable, the Son of Man sows good seed, and the devil sows weeds among it. True and false believers grow side by side in this age and cannot always be told apart, but at the final harvest God will separate them perfectly. Jesus also spoke of himself as a grain of wheat that must fall into the ground and die, so as to bear much fruit. Matthew 13:25 but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. An enemy deliberately sowed weeds that would look like wheat. Matthew 13:30 Let both grow together until the harvest Final separation belongs to God at the end of the age. John 12:24 unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Christ’s death is the seed of a great harvest.

Cedars of Lebanon The cedars of Lebanon were huge, long-lived evergreen trees from the mountains north of Israel, prized for their strong, fragrant timber. What it was. The cedar of Lebanon grows on the high slopes of the Lebanon mountains. It can reach about 100 to 130 feet (30 to 40 m), with a massive trunk and wide, spreading branches, and it can live for over a thousand years. Its reddish wood is strong, sweet-smelling and resists rot and insects. Kings across the ancient world sent for it. Solomon traded with Hiram king of Tyre for cedar logs, floated down the coast in rafts, to build the temple and his palace. In today’s terms. A full-grown cedar can stand as tall as a ten-storey building. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because they were so tall and strong, cedars were a picture of human pride and power, which God can break with a word. They were also a picture of the righteous, who “grow like a cedar in Lebanon”, flourishing in God’s house. The temple’s cedar-lined walls pointed to the beauty and permanence of God’s dwelling, fulfilled in Christ and his people. 1 Kings 5:6 Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. Solomon imported cedar for the temple. Psalm 29:5 The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon. Even the mightiest trees are nothing before God’s power. Psalm 92:12 The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. The righteous are pictured as strong, flourishing trees.

Thorns and Thistles Thorns and thistles are prickly weeds and shrubs, common in Israel, which the Bible treats as a sign of the curse on the ground after the fall. What it was. Israel has dozens of kinds of thorny plants, from low thistles in the fields to thorn bushes used as hedges and as quick fuel for fires. They spread wherever land was neglected and choked crops if not cleared. Farmers had to fight them constantly. Thorn branches were also used to make fences around sheepfolds and vineyards. In today’s terms. Think of brambles and nettles taking over an abandoned garden, only sharper. Why it matters when you read the Bible. After Adam’s sin, God said the ground would bring forth “thorns and thistles”: work became toil. In the parable of the sower, thorns stand for the cares and riches that choke God’s word. Then at his trial the soldiers twisted thorns into a crown for Jesus. The King wore the very sign of the curse on his head, because he was bearing the curse for us, so that creation and his people might be set free. Genesis 3:18 thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field. Thorns are part of the curse that came with sin. Matthew 13:7 Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Thorns picture the worries and riches that choke faith. Matthew 27:29 and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head Christ was crowned with the sign of the curse he came to bear.

Sheep and Goats Sheep and goats were the main flock animals of Israel, kept for wool, hair, milk, meat and sacrifice. What it was. Flocks often included both animals, grazing together by day. Sheep, many with broad fat tails, gave wool and meat. They are timid, easily lost and helpless against predators. Goats, usually black, gave milk and long hair woven into tent cloth and sackcloth. They are hardy and independent, and climb and browse on shrubs. At night shepherds might separate them, since goats need more warmth. Lambs and young goats were the most common animals sacrificed. In today’s terms. A family’s flock was its bank account, larder and clothing supply all in one. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Isaiah says “All we like sheep have gone astray”: we wander like helpless sheep. Yet the Lord laid our sin on his Servant, the Lamb of God. On the Day of Atonement one goat was sacrificed and another, the scapegoat, carried Israel’s sins away into the wilderness. At the last judgment Christ will divide people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Isaiah 53:6 All we like sheep have gone astray Wandering sheep picture sinners, whose sin the Lord laid on his Servant. Matthew 25:32 and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. A familiar farm task pictures the final judgment.

Donkey and Colt The donkey was the everyday working animal of Israel, used for riding and carrying loads, and a colt was a young donkey. What it was. Donkeys were strong, sure-footed and cheap to keep, able to carry heavy loads on hilly roads. Almost every family that could afford one had one. People of rank also rode them in times of peace: judges’ sons rode donkeys, and David’s mule carried Solomon to be crowned. Horses, by contrast, were mainly for war and chariots, and Israel’s kings were warned not to multiply them. A colt that had never been ridden was fit for a special, holy use. In today’s terms. A donkey was the family van and tractor; a war horse was a tank. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Balaam’s donkey saw the angel her master could not. Zechariah foretold Israel’s King coming “humble and mounted on a donkey”, not on a war horse. Jesus fulfilled this on Palm Sunday, riding into Jerusalem on a colt. He came as a King of peace, humble and bringing salvation, on his way to the cross. Zechariah 9:9 Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. The promised King would come in humility and peace. Mark 11:7 And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. Jesus deliberately fulfilled Zechariah’s prophecy. Numbers 22:28 Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey God can even use a donkey to rebuke a stubborn prophet.

Locusts Locusts are large grasshoppers that can gather in vast swarms and strip a whole land of every green thing. What it was. Most of the time desert locusts live alone, but after good rains they can multiply and form huge swarms that fly with the wind. A single swarm may contain hundreds of millions of insects and cover many square miles, darkening the sky. Each locust eats roughly its own weight in plants every day, so they can leave fields, vineyards and trees bare in hours. The law allowed Israel to eat certain locusts, and poor people did, roasted or dried. In today’s terms. A large swarm can eat as much food in a day as tens of thousands of people. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Locusts were the eighth plague on Egypt, and Joel describes a locust plague as a warning of the coming day of the Lord. Yet God also promises, “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten.” John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey, the plain food of the wilderness, as he prepared the way for Christ. Exodus 10:14 such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again. God used locusts as a judgment on Egypt. Joel 1:4 What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. Wave after wave of locusts left nothing behind. Matthew 3:4 and his food was locusts and wild honey. Locusts were plain food for those living in the wilderness.

Dove Doves and pigeons were common birds in Israel, offered as sacrifices by the poor and seen as gentle and harmless. What it was. Several kinds of dove lived in the land, including the rock dove (the wild pigeon) and the turtledove, which migrates and returns in spring. They were easy to keep and cheap to buy. The law allowed people who could not afford a lamb to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead, and dove-sellers did business in the temple courts. Doves were seen as gentle, innocent birds, faithful to their mates. In today’s terms. A pair of pigeons was the cheapest sacrifice in the law, the poor family’s offering. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Noah’s dove returned with an olive leaf, a sign that judgment was over. Mary and Joseph offered two birds when Jesus was presented, showing they were poor. At Jesus’ baptism the Spirit came down “like a dove”, gentle and peaceful, resting on him as the anointed Messiah. Jesus sent his disciples out “innocent as doves”. Genesis 8:11 And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. The dove brought the first sign of new life after the flood. Luke 2:24 a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. Jesus’ parents brought the poor family’s offering. Matthew 3:16 and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; The Spirit came on Jesus gently and visibly at his baptism.

Lion Lions lived wild in the land of Israel in Bible times, and they were the Bible’s chief picture of strength, danger and royal power. What it was. The lions of Bible lands were Asian lions, a little smaller than African lions. They lived in the thickets along the Jordan and in wild hill country, and attacked flocks and sometimes people. They survived in the region until about the time of the Crusades. Shepherds like David had to fight them off. Kings, including the kings of Persia, kept lions in pits or enclosures, and carved lions guarded thrones, as at Solomon’s throne. In today’s terms. A lion could weigh as much as two or three grown men and was the most feared animal in the land. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Samson and David killed lions by God’s strength, and Daniel was kept safe in a den of lions. Peter warns that the devil prowls like a roaring lion. But the true Lion is Christ, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, as Jacob foretold. And when John turns to see that Lion, he sees a Lamb that has been slain: Christ conquered by dying for us. Daniel 6:22 My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not harmed me God protected Daniel from the most feared beast of all. 1 Peter 5:8 Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. The lion pictures the danger Satan poses to believers. Revelation 5:5 behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered Christ is the royal Lion who has won the victory.

Leaven (Yeast) Leaven was a piece of old fermented dough kept back from one batch of bread and mixed into the next to make it rise. What it was. There were no packets of dried yeast. Instead the baker saved a lump of sour, fermented dough (rather like a sourdough starter today) and worked it into fresh flour and water. Slowly and unseen it spread through the whole batch and made it rise. At Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Israel had to clear every bit of leaven out of their houses and eat flat, unleavened bread for seven days, remembering how they left Egypt in haste. In today’s terms. Leaven worked like a sourdough starter: a small piece changes the whole loaf. The woman in Jesus’ parable used three measures of flour, probably around 40 pounds (18 kg), enough bread for a hundred people or more. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Because a little leaven spreads through everything, it usually pictures sin and false teaching (“the leaven of the Pharisees”). Paul tells the church to clear out the old leaven, because Christ our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed. Yet Jesus also used leaven positively: the kingdom of heaven works quietly through the world until it fills it all. Exodus 12:15 On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses Removing leaven was part of keeping the Passover. 1 Corinthians 5:7 Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Leaven pictures sin that must be cleared out because of Christ’s sacrifice. Matthew 13:33 The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened. Here leaven pictures the hidden, unstoppable spread of God’s kingdom.

Salt Salt was essential in the ancient world for flavouring and preserving food, and it was required with Israel’s offerings as a sign of a lasting covenant. What it was. Much of Israel’s salt came from the shores of the Dead Sea, where it was gathered from pools and rocks. Without refrigeration, salt was the main way to keep meat and fish from going bad. It was also rubbed on newborn babies and used in medicine. Dead Sea salt was often mixed with other minerals; if damp got into it, the true salt could dissolve away, leaving a tasteless white powder that was thrown onto paths. Eating salt together sealed friendship, and “a covenant of salt” meant a lasting, unbreakable one. In today’s terms. Salt was the refrigerator and the seasoning of the ancient kitchen. Why it matters when you read the Bible. Every grain offering had to be seasoned with “the salt of the covenant”, a reminder that God keeps his promises for ever. Jesus calls his disciples “the salt of the earth”: their lives are to hold back the decay of the world and give it a taste of God’s goodness. And Paul wants Christians’ speech to be “seasoned with salt”, gracious and worth hearing. Leviticus 2:13 You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering Salt stood for the lasting faithfulness of God’s covenant. Matthew 5:13 You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? Christ’s people are to make a real difference in the world. Colossians 4:6 Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt Gracious, wise speech is like well-seasoned food.
